detail.abstract: Leading explanations of the backlash against globalization center on grievance and status threat-particularly among white natives toward those perceived as foreign at home and abroad. Yet the politics of backlash against trade and immigration are typically studied separately. Critically, U.S. immigration politics are also racialized and inseparable from Latino politics. To explain these interrelated phenomena, we highlight that local exposure to trade competition can be distributed differently across groups. We argue that relative economic decline of a dominant group triggers status threat and shapes political behavior. In short, who is exposed matters. We examine the white-Hispanic gap in local exposure to Chinese imports across US commuting zones from 2000 to 2024. A larger gap increases support for Republican presidential candidates. This effect is concentrated where local exposure to hostile immigration rhetoric is greatest. Additional analysis of labor market outcomes and anti-Latino sentiment supports status threat as the mechanism. We thank Jude Hays and participants of the 2026 Pitt/Penn State IR Workshop for feedback.

detail.title: A Centralized Fiat Digital Currency System with Forced-Circulation Currencies

detail.abstract: Existing digital currency practice-Bitcoin and stablecoins-is characterized by decentralization, with issuance and governance beyond the control of national monetary authorities. This paper proposes a centralized fiat digital currency system consisting of two classes of money: conventional currency (cash and conventional digital currency, freely circulating and freely exchangeable) and special-purpose currency (also called special digital currency or special currency): for policy purposes, the government exploits the advantages of digital technology to attach various restrictions to the circulation conditions of money, so that it can circulate only under specified circumstances. Whether a special-purpose currency should be issued depends on whether the benefits brought by the restrictions significantly outweigh the drawbacks. A special-purpose currency may carry rules such as holding deadlines (forced circulation), circulation taxes, tags, and redemption thresholds, achieving policy functions that traditional monetary instruments find difficult to accomplish without changing the total money supply. currency is also easy. The paper then presents three examples of forced-circulation currencies: the R-coin (consumption-boosting), the X-coin (innovation-boosting), and the F-coin (fiscal relief). The special-purpose currencies proposed in this paper already go, to some extent, beyond the framework of traditional centralized money, opening a new direction for modern monetary theory and extending political economy. This direction combines depth in fundamental theory with direct policy value-a wholly new field with enormous potential impact. It can be asserted that in the future someone will surely win the Nobel Prize in Economics in this direction.

detail.abstract: Indian banks remain among the least scrutinised sources of financed emissions despite their lending portfolios carrying a substantial carbon burden. This paper provides scope-disaggregated estimates of the carbon intensity of Indian bank loans using the Environmentally Extended Input-Output (EEIO) framework. Unlike prior studies, we construct sector-specific emission intensities from the ground up to produce estimates that are transparent, reproducible, and resistant to greenwashing. The choice of emissions scope turns out to matter enormously. Under Scope 1, the electricity sector dominates measured emissions, and Public-Sector Banks (PSBs), with their heavy exposure to power generation, record the highest carbon intensity of loans (CIL). Under final energy emissions (Scope 1 + Scope 2 minus electricity sector), that PSB premium largely disappears as emissions are redistributed to end-use sectors. Under Scope 3 (supply chain emissions), seemingly low-carbon sectors such as construction, hospitality, telecommunications emerge as hidden hotspots. Across all three approaches, CIL declined meaningfully between 2012-13 and 2022-23, with the sharpest fall under Scope 3 (34.4 per cent, from 175.7 to 115.2 tCO₂ per crore). These findings carry direct implications for climate risk supervision. Scope selection is not a technical footnote - it determines which banks appear high-risk and how decarbonisation strategies are prioritised. For financial institutions operating in data-scarce environments, the EEIO approach offers a scalable, verifiable baseline for financed emissions disclosure, one that India's evolving climate finance framework urgently needs.

title: The Impact of Projection Contamination on Macroeconomic Panel Data Analysis

detail.abstract: Current-vintage macroeconomic databases can place realized observations and institutional projections in the same rectangular panel. This note shows that treating both as observations changes the regression estimand. After fixed effects and controls are partialled out, a mixed-vintage regression omits the interaction between the regressor and projection status. The probability limit equals the realized-data slope plus a leverage-weighted projection-regime gap. Hence a short-projected tail can generate a large bias when it has high regressor leverage, and conventional tests of the realized-data null can reject with probability approaching one. A status-aware augmented regression and an actual-only estimator recover the realized-data target under transparent conditions. Monte Carlo panels of 150 units over 1980-2025 match the analytical bias almost exactly. The April-2026 IMF World Economic Outlook illustrates why status must be defined country-by-series rather than by a common calendar cutoff.

detail.abstract: Several digital payment innovations, such as stablecoins, have emerged with a promise to bring developmental benefits, but their relevance for financial inclusion have not been explored in the literature. This study explores the role of stablecoins in increasing financial inclusion in countries. It shows that stablecoins enhances financial inclusion by offering an alternative to bank accounts, lowering transaction cost, removing financial intermediaries to increase the level of financial inclusion, increasing competition to serve underserved adults, offering worldwide access to the underlying financial assets backing the stablecoin, and greater access to on-chain savings. The risks associated with using stablecoins to increase financial inclusion include the potential for de-pegging, currency substitution, illicit financing, lack of regulatory support, technological barriers and very little consumer protection for stablecoin holders.

title: Environmental policy uncertainty and cleantech FDI
affiliations: and Geneva Graduate Institute

detail.title: Environmental policy uncertainty and cleantech FDI
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether environmental policy uncertainty undermines clean-technology investment in the United States by weakening policy-induced investment incentives. Using quarterly project-level data on U.S. greenfield investments from 2007Q1 to 2019Q1, combined with novel news-based indices that separately measure environmental policy salience and environmental policy uncertainty, we find that policy uncertainty substantially offsets the positive investment effects of environmental policy. At the aggregate level, a one-standard-deviation increase in environmental policy uncertainty eliminates roughly 75% of the policy-induced increase in the number of cleantech projects and around 50% of the increase in capital expenditure. The deterrence effect is substantially stronger for foreign than for domestic investors, consistent with greater informational frictions facing cross-border capital. These effects persist for at least two years following an uncertainty shock and are corroborated by country- and firm-level analyses, though results for capital expenditure are less robust at disaggregated levels. The findings imply that policy credibility is a first-order determinant of clean investment: an environmental policy framework that is ambitious but perceived as unstable may fail to mobilize the capital it is designed to attract.

title: Home Rule, Local Autonomy, and Voters: Explaining Government Growth
affiliations: Schoool of Public Affairs, Arizona State University

detail.title: Home Rule, Local Autonomy, and Voters: Explaining Government Growth

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: This paper examines local government growth by analyzing how municipalities respond to increases in taxing autonomy and whether their responses are conditioned on voter preferences. Specifically, we investigate the fiscal impact of home rule when the shift to home rule status (HRS) is independent of voter preferences versus when voters adopt home rule. We find that home rule has no effect on tax collections when changes in HRS are unrelated to voter preferences. However, the tax structure shifts to one that more closely aligns with the preferences of the median voter. In contrast, when voters select into HRS there is a significant and sustained increase in tax revenues that is driven by increases in property and sales taxes. These findings indicate that local fiscal policy is responsive to the preferences of the median voter.

title:
The Civilizational Complexity Report: 
Civilizational Intelligibility, Mediation, and the Scaling of Complexity
affiliations: Independent

detail.title:
The Civilizational Complexity Report: 
Civilizational Intelligibility, Mediation, and the Scaling of Complexity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial or personal relationships with other individuals or organizations that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, this research. The report was developed as part of the author's independent research programme in Productisation Studies through the Institute of Productisation.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
The Civilizational Complexity Report establishes a civilizational research problem that is broader than any single AI failure mode and more fundamental than the present debate over whether machines are “intelligent.” Civilization has always depended on mediation: capabilities, distinctions, procedures, authority, memory and relationships must be carried across people, places, generations and increasingly complex systems. As capability is amplified, the complexity carried by mediators also increases. The unresolved question is whether the mediator remains sufficiently intelligible to preserve the state that makes the capability recognizable, usable, coordinable, governable and inheritable.

This report argues that the contemporary AI transition makes this problem unusually visible. AI systems do not merely store or retrieve information; they select, compress, reconstruct, synthesize, route and increasingly operationalize accumulated human representations. The resulting system can amplify capability while weakening the intelligibility of the states from which that capability derives. This condition is described here as a Mediator Intelligibility Gap: a structural mismatch between the complexity a mediator is required to carry and the descriptive, operational, coordination and accumulative intelligibility it can preserve at the relevant scale.

The report therefore repositions the Civilizational Complexity Report. The eighteen pressure surfaces introduced by this report form the observational register, but they are reorganized around a higher-order thesis: civilizational complexity becomes dangerous when mediators are asked to carry states they can no longer adequately represent. The issue is visible in machine-readable identity, attribution, provenance, EEAT erosion, zero-click value evaporation, role ambiguity, knowledge fragmentation, coordination deficits and the accumulation of weakly qualified representations. These are treated as related manifestations of mediator inadequacy, not as isolated platform problems.

The report also clarifies the relationship of the broader Productisation Studies programme to this problem. Productisation addresses the conversion of capability into bounded, attributable, transferable and persistent form; Constraint Productisation Theory addresses the integrity of constraints under amplification; DOC+AL provides an observation structure for Description, Operation, Coordination and Accumulation; State Boxes are proposed as ontology-bearing state objects; Productised Knowledge Graphs provide accumulative traversability; and Structural Productisation Security names the security condition sought when amplified mediation must remain intelligible. The Productisation Imperative supplies the economic mandate to preserve capability and its source through mediation.

The report concludes with a founding research programme and test agenda. It does not claim that every proposed framework is validated. It does establish that civilization now faces a common research question: how can mediators be made sufficiently intelligible to carry the complexity that civilization is increasingly capable of generating?

title: A Practical Legal Guide to Drilling Rig Ownership, Local Content and Cabotage Compliance in Nigeria

detail.title: A Practical Legal Guide to Drilling Rig Ownership, Local Content and Cabotage Compliance in Nigeria

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Personal funding

detail.abstract:
Oil drilling rigs are among the most valuable assets in Nigeria’s upstream petroleum industry. They facilitate exploration, appraisal, development, and production drilling, making them indispensable to Nigeria's oil and gas sector. As Nigeria seeks to increase indigenous participation through local content policies while still trying to attract investment into upstream petroleum operations, ownership and operation of drilling rigs have become increasingly regulated in recent years.

Prospective investors, drilling contractors, and operators must understand and navigate a complex legal and regulatory landscape that extends beyond the Petroleum Industry Act, 2021 (the “PIA”). Ownership and operation of drilling rigs are governed by a wide range of legal regimes, including local content requirements, maritime regulations, customs laws, environmental obligations, labour standards, and taxation. Failure to comply with the requirements under these different regulatory frameworks may result in project delays, financial penalties, loss of business opportunities, regulatory sanctions, or even outright blacklisting from participating in drilling operations in the sector.

In this article, we provide a practical overview of the legal considerations surrounding oil drilling rig ownership and related local content compliance in Nigeria's petroleum regulatory environment. It focuses primarily on rig ownership structures, Nigerian content requirements, NCRC eligibility, and Cabotage implications for offshore rigs that qualify as vessels. Other compliance issues, such as tax, customs, environmental, HSE, and immigration obligations, are noted only where they interact with ownership and local content structuring. The article does not attempt to provide an exhaustive treatment of every regulatory approval required for drilling operations, but highlights the issues most relevant to ownership structuring, market entry, and local content compliance.

title: Utility-level-dependent Ambiguity
affiliations: University of Southampton

detail.title: Utility-level-dependent Ambiguity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Experimental evidence suggests that ambiguity-sensitive choice can vary systematically with the circumstances of a decision. This paper isolates one channel within a stable preference relation: ambiguity weighting may depend on the act's certainty-equivalent level. After the standard Anscombe-Aumann calibration of consequence utility, a set of behavioral axioms yields a unique continuous family of normalized monotone capacities  $\{\nu_v\}_{v\in(0,1)}$. Each nonendpoint act is evaluated by the Choquet integral associated with the capacity at its own interior certainty-equivalent level, while nonendpoint acts on the same indifference surface share the same capacity. Binary event comparisons identify local event weights at each elicited level and trace their cross-level variation, providing tests of the fixed-capacity restriction. Local uncertainty aversion is equivalent to convexity of ν v and yields an implicit multiple-priors representation with certainty-equivalent-indexed local cores. Certainty translation invariance holds if and only if the capacity is fixed across levels, recovering the maintained nondegenerate fixed-capacity Choquet expected utility benchmark; global mixture-betweenness yields implicit additive utility, and imposing both restrictions recovers full-support subjective expected utility. The capacity schedule is a reduced-form ambiguity weighting whose variation may reflect changes in ambiguity perception, ambiguity attitude, or both.

title: Corporate Ownership, Purpose, and the Social Choice Problem
affiliations: Wharton School, University of Penn and University of Utah

detail.title: Corporate Ownership, Purpose, and the Social Choice Problem

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This conceptual paper did not involve human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Firms face social choice problems whenever the participants on whose cooperation they rely hold incommensurable values. We discuss how owners occupy a distinctive dual role in this context: they are both participants with values of their own and the arbiters that determine how social choice problems are resolved. Corporate purpose is one important instrument through which owners exercise this authority. By committing the firm to problems they aim to solve, purpose restricts the domain of preferences the firm must reconcile and signals a preference ordering to employees and other participants. The firm's composition is a second instrument. Because firms can alter their membership through hiring and termination, owners assemble coalitions whose values sustain the chosen purpose, constrained by employees' capacity to exercise voice or exit. This chapter therefore expands corporate governance beyond mitigating agency issues by describing its central role in framing how firms resolve their social choice problems.
Firms are problem-solving institutions that provide the coordination required to solve complex
problems—problems that markets are less suited to resolve on their own (Nickerson & Zenger,
2004). In this context, corporate purpose can be considered as the problems that firms choose to
address and how they will be solved (Gartenberg & Zenger, 2023). As firms scale and increase in
complexity, however, they face a fundamental challenge: aligning the preferences of the diverse
actors engaged in this problem-solving. These preferences are not only monetary or instrumental
in nature but also reflect the deeper values held by these actors (Bénabou & Tirole, 2026). As a
result, the central challenge of the firm is not only to coordinate knowledge and to align incentives,
but also to align divergent values among the actors on whose cooperation the firm depends.
This challenge is particularly acute because many organizational considerations cannot be
translated cleanly into a financial numeraire. Take the example of an artificial intelligence lab that
considers safety and alignment important factors influencing both social welfare and long-run
value, as are speed and flexibility. A dispute over whether safety should constrain either of those
is also a dispute over what the organization ought to do and cannot be addressed using financial
logic alone.
This is the central problem of social choice theory. Arrow’s Impossibility Theorem (Arrow, 1951)
formalized the difficulty of aggregating incommensurable preferences into a coherent collective
ordering without violating reasonable fairness conditions. While the insight is usually applied to
societies at large and public decision-making, firms internalize this difficulty when they require
cooperation among participants who hold different values. Corporate governance therefore has a
broader role than the standard agency view suggests. In addition to monitoring and rewarding
agents, it is responsible for resolving contested social-choice problems that underpin many
important decisions by organizations.

title: Does Competition Improve Information Quality: Evidence from the Security Analyst Market
affiliations: University of Toulouse Capitole - Toulouse School of Economics

detail.title: Does Competition Improve Information Quality: Evidence from the Security Analyst Market

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare that I have no conflicts of interest, no funding from a related party, and no other material financial interests related to the submission.
declarations.funderStatement: I acknowledge funding from ANR under grant ANR-17-EURE-0010 (Investissements d’Avenir program).

detail.abstract: Experts are often rewarded for relative performance. For security analysts, this turns forecasting stocks into a contest in which analysts compete to be more accurate than their peers. The contest can induce analysts to distort their forecasts to stand out, but can also discipline them against issuing overly optimistic forecasts-a central concern of policymakers in this market. I develop and structurally estimate a forecasting contest model, inferring analysts' incentives from their forecasts using a revealed-preference approach. The model incorporates relative-accuracy and optimism incentives in a unified framework, enabling counterfactual simulations that speak to recent policy debates over optimism and analyst competition. I find that the incentives interact, leading analysts with bullish signals to disproportionately exaggerate them. Under the estimated incentives, the contest nevertheless acts as a "market-based" discipline on optimism, reducing forecast errors overall even as its interaction with optimism amplifies forecast noise. The estimated model implies that aggregate information quality is inverted-U-shaped in the number of competing analysts: additional competition produces more information but also intensifies contest-driven distortions.

title: Summer of Discontent, A Political Economy Perspective of Recent Regime Change in West Bengal
affiliations: University of Burdwan

detail.title: Summer of Discontent, A Political Economy Perspective of Recent Regime Change in West Bengal

declarations.funderStatement: The author did not receive financial support from any organization for the submitted work.

detail.abstract: A regime change happened in West Bengal in the summer of 2026 when the Bharatiya Janata Party ended the fifteen year rule of All India Trinamool Congress comprehensively. Traditionally electors in Bengal have preferred status-quo and the state has a history of longserving regimes, upturned only by momentous events like the Naxalite movement, the Emergency, the Singur land movement or the police brutality at Nandigram. Against this backdrop, the present paper attempts to explain the regime change using a political economy perspective of patronage, fiscal constraints, opposition mobilisation, and survival conditions. We show that survival of a regime dependent on patronage is self-destructive in the long run due to crowding out of legitimate economic activities unless new avenues for employment generation and revenue collection can be found. The headroom squeezes further if external sources of funds dry up. The framework and the results of the model match with the realities in Bengal.

title: Cross-industry M&A as Response to Industry Maturity and Declining Growth
affiliations: , KIIT University and KIIT University

detail.title: Cross-industry M&A as Response to Industry Maturity and Declining Growth

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known personal, professional, or financial conflicts of interest that could have influenced or could be perceived to have influenced the research presented in this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: As industries advance in their life cycles, most of them eventually go into a state of maturity characterized by gradual growth, market saturation, and mounting competitive pressures. In these contexts, companies are usually forced to venture beyond conventional strategies to maintain performance and guarantee long-term existence. One such reaction has been the quest for cross-industry mergers and acquisitions (M&A), through which companies can diversify into new markets, gain access to novel technologies, and mitigate oversubscription to fading markets. Crossindustry M&A differs from horizontal or vertical integration in that it broadens a company's strategic vistas by tying it to industries with alternative growth paths, bases of consumers, and business models. This abstract analyses cross-industry M&A as a strategic reaction to industry maturity and shrinking growth based on industrial organization theory, diversification theory, and the resource-based view. Central motivations that are cited are seeking disruptive innovation, risk diversification, and synergy-hunting across unrelated industries. The challenges of cultural integration, overestimation of synergies, and regulatory issues, however, highlight the complexity of these transactions. Case studies of deals like Amazon's takeover of Whole Foods and Facebook's acquisition of Oculus highlight how companies use cross-industry M&A to position themselves anew in changing markets. The argument here is that with dynamic capabilities and a strategic vision, cross-industry M&A can be more than a tactical response to decline; it can be a renewing force in competition and a means of sustainable growth.

title: Shifting currents: China’s import realignment
affiliations: Bank of Finland,  and Bank of Finland - Institute for Economies in Transition (BOFIT)

detail.title: Shifting currents: China’s import realignment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Finland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether China has reallocated import sourcing away from West-leaning economies amid heightened geoeconomic tensions and a policy push to strengthen supply chain security. Using monthly bilateral trade data for 121 economies over 2015–2025 and a difference-in-differences framework, we compare changes in countries’ shares of China’s imports across blocs defined by their official positioning on Taiwan. We find evidence of a relative decline in imports from Westleaning countries beginning in 2018, with divergence strengthening after 2020 and intensifying further in 2022. The pattern is concentrated on a limited set of rawmaterial sectors, especially mineral products and base metals. For goods covered by Western export controls to Russia, we find no evidence of a broader shift in China’s sourcing. Overall, China’s import realignment appears broad-based across West-leaning source countries, but has so far remained selective across product categories. China’s shift toward importing from friendly nations is likely to contribute to larger bilateral trade surpluses with Western economies, provided that China’s exports to these markets remain robust.

title: Cut off from capital: the impacts of sanctions on portfolio investments
affiliations: Bank of Finland - Institute for Economies in Transition (BOFIT) and Bank of Finland - Institute for Economies in Transition (BOFIT)

detail.title: Cut off from capital: the impacts of sanctions on portfolio investments

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Finland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine the impact from sanctions on global capital flows. Sanctions can be understood as an extreme version of geopolitical decoupling that affects economic relations, including trade and foreign direct investment. Specifically, we look at how the introduction of wide-ranging financial sanctions has affected foreign portfolio investment, treating Western sanctions packages on Russia in 2014 and 2022 as a natural experiment. Applying a triple-difference setup and using annual portfolio investment data collected by the IMF, our results show that portfolio investment flows into Russia sharply declined from both sanctioning and non-sanctioning countries particularly after 2022. The decline in investment from sanctioning countries was much more severe, however. Unlike with trade, we find little evidence of investment diversion for Russia after imposition of sanctions.

detail.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence allows firms to delegate multi-step sequences of work rather than isolated tasks. We argue that delegated machine execution can separate the portability of production from the portability of validation: execution may become technically portable while the evidence required to validate it remains organizationally specific. We conceptualize process evidence as a metering mechanism for process fidelity and process-evidence specificity as a relational transaction attribute distinct from productive-asset or execution-technology specificity. Three relationships follow. Holding trace completeness constant, metering improves when consequential execution events are linked to independently specified authorization criteria. A wider execution–evidence portability gap increases accountability-burden exposure; endogenous governance can attenuate the burden ultimately retained. Where formal answerability is institutionally transferable, the same mechanism also makes outward transfer of accountability less likely. Greater process-evidence specificity shifts governance away from arm’s-length contracting, while the dominant evidence cost predicts safeguard selection. The framework applies most strongly to consequential multi-step work where final outputs imperfectly reveal process fidelity and authorized baselines are sufficiently stable for comparison. The paper extends theory-of-the-firm reasoning by identifying validation evidence as a transaction-relevant object that can remain co-specialized with the accountable organization even when execution technology is standardized.

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the Singapore Ministry of Education (MOE) Tier 1 Grants titled \textit{The Internet-of-Buildings (IoB) Platform -- Testing of Visual Analytics for AI Technologies towards a Well and Green Built Environment} (A-0008305-01-00) and Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) for Built Environment Research (A0008301-01-00).

detail.abstract: The everyday experience of urban space is shaped as much by how people perceive heat, noise, and their social surroundings as by the physical conditions that sensors record. This paper characterizes how that lived experience differs across the common spaces of a dense tropical city using crowdsourced, watch-based micro-surveys collected with the open-source Cozie smartwatch platform. A field deployment in Singapore with 106 participants produced 9,962 geolocated micro-survey responses, each pairing self-reported thermal preference, noise, social context, and activity with the wearer's onboard physiological signals and with linked outdoor weather. Every response included a self-reported location in one of six everyday space types, and the reported experience was characterized through conditional perception fingerprints, relative distinctiveness expressed as lift, and effect-size-based association testing using the chi-square statistic, Cramér's V, and adjusted standardized residuals. The strongest separations between spaces are behavioral and acoustic rather than thermal, as what a person is doing and hearing identifies a space more sharply (Cramér's V up to 0.38) than how warm they feel (0.12). Commute spaces carry the loudest and most traffic-driven noise, indoor spaces are defined by talking, and cooling demand is lowest in air-conditioned offices and highest outdoors, while thermal preference tracks the immediate controlled environment more than the outdoor weather. These findings show that a scalable smartwatch micro-survey can recover and quantify the perceptual signature of everyday urban spaces, offering a human-centered evidence base for noise mitigation and for energy-conscious, thermal comfort-aware urban design in tropical cities.

title: The Flight to Affordability: Effects of Pandemic Rent Increases on Renters By Geography
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Independent, Independent, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Independent and Independent

detail.title: The Flight to Affordability: Effects of Pandemic Rent Increases on Renters By Geography

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 2026-062, 2026[10.17016/FEDS.2026.062]

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: In the pandemic era, people moved from high-density, expensive areas to more affordable areas, putting upward pressure on local housing prices. We examine the geographic distribution of rent growth during this time and its effects on renters. We use administrative new lease data from RealPage and household-level data on rent and income from the American Community Survey. We analyze rents and incomes using Public Use Microdata Areas grouped in two ways: by prepandemic rent levels and by pre-pandemic rent-to-income ratios. Rents grew more in areas with lower pre-pandemic rents but not in areas with lower rent-to-income ratios, consistent with higher-income remote workers moving away from high rent areas to more affordable areas. Lower-income households experienced larger increases in rent relative to their income compared to the median renter. However, area-level rent-to-income ratios reflect both compositional changes in renter populations from mobility and changes in local rents. We highlight the need for future work to track affordability for the same households over time to fully understand pandemic era affordability trends.

detail.title: Investment under fire: Firm responses to war in Ukraine

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Finland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: How do firms adapt their decision-making about strategic investments during a war? We examine this question in the context of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, combining data on almost 500,000 Ukrainian firms from 2017 to 2023 with detailed conflict data. We argue that war reshapes firm investment through three related mechanisms: exposure to violence, changes in the strategic value of firm resources, and sectoral alignment with wartime demand. Our results show that firms exposed to war strongly reduce their investment, and that this negative investment response is amplified by conflict intensity. Moreover, war reconfigures the strategic value of firm resources: financial resilience preserves firm investments, whereas the investment advantages associated with firm size and leverage weaken as larger firms have more resources at risk and debt creates financial rigidity. Firms in war-related industries increase investment during war, indicating that productive capabilities aligned with wartime demand may create strategic opportunities even under extreme uncertainty. These findings contribute to research on violent conflict and firm strategy by showing that war is not simply a uniform negative shock, but also creates a strategic context in which firms adapt depending on how risks, resources, and opportunities are reconfigured.

detail.abstract: National dialogue has increasingly become an important instrument for addressing political crises, violent conflict, institutional weaknesses, social divisions, and contested questions of national identity and governance. Unlike conventional peace negotiations, which are often limited to armed groups or political elites, a national dialogue seeks to create a broader political and social platform through which diverse stakeholders can discuss fundamental national issues and develop consensual solutions. Ethiopia is one of the countries that has recently undergone a national dialogue aimed at addressing its deeply rooted political and social conflicts. This manuscript evaluates the strengths and weaknesses of the Ethiopian National Dialogue with regard to its institutional arrangements, participation mechanisms, and methodologies. The paper adopts a qualitative methodology based primarily on document analysis, institutional reports, and the individual observations of the author as a delegate who participated in the process. The paper demonstrates that the process exhibited major strengths, particularly with respect to the political will of the government, the credibility of the convener, broad public participation, the relevance, clarity, and comprehensiveness of proposed agenda items, and a structured deliberative methodology that involved experts and progressed from micro-groups to larger strategic groups.

detail.title: When Is a Balance Test Misleading? Standardized Differences versus t-Tests in Large Matched Administrative Panels

detail.abstract: After matching, researchers routinely check whether the intervention and control groups are comparable on observed covariates. Two diagnostics dominate practice: the standardized mean difference (SMD) and the two-sample t-test. These diagnostics can disagree sharply, and the disagreement is not random; it is driven by sample size. Using a real matched panel of firms drawn from a large administrative database (roughly 2.4 million matched pairs), we subsample the matched data at sizes ranging from 100 to the full sample and, at each size, compute both diagnostics for continuous covariates over one hundred random draws. The SMD stays well below the conventional 0.10 threshold across the entire range and moves only modestly with sample size: for log total assets it settles near 0.041, and for employment it settles near 0.004 as the sample grows, a difference of no practical consequence. The t-test behaves in the opposite way. At a few hundred observations it almost never rejects; by ten thousand it rejects the null of equal means in nearly every draw; at the full sample it rejects every time, including for the employment covariate whose imbalance is negligible by any substantive standard. The lesson for practitioners is direct: in large administrative panels in a large sample the t-test answers a question about sample size rather than about balance, and reporting it as evidence of imbalance is misleading. We close with a short checklist for choosing and reporting balance diagnostics.

detail.abstract: We analyze the effects of both optimal and actual tariff-escalation policies in a twocountry general-equilibrium trade model with occupational choice, offshoring, and unemployment. Calibrating the model to reflect key economic conditions in the US and China before the tariff wars started, we find that optimal (Nash equilibrium) tariffs lead to a decline in welfare for both countries, an increase in unemployment in the US and a decrease in China, and a rise in top-income inequality in both countries. Furthermore, our analysis shows that neither the US nor China emerged victorious from the tariff wars from 2018 through 2025.

title: The Nonlinear Cost of Consolidated Action: From Coordination to Hypercontrol
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Nonlinear Cost of Consolidated Action: From Coordination to Hypercontrol

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known financial or personal relationships that could have influenced, or could be perceived to have influenced, the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This theoretical study did not involve human participants, personal data, animals, or experimental interventions requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Centralization works. Sometimes it works spectacularly. It can turn several priorities into a common vector, align people and financial resources behind them, and complete projects that dispersed actors might never attempt. The harder question is not whether centralization works. It is when it stops working.

This paper locates that boundary. Consolidation remains productive while the marginal benefit of a common vector is greater than the marginal cost of lost local autonomy. It turns destructive when the next unit of alignment suppresses more independent initiative, experimentation, and responsibility than it saves in coordination cost.

The boundary moves with the geometry of the task. Several visible and rankable directions can tolerate substantial consolidation. A field containing thousands or millions of heterogeneous, local, and changing directions cannot. The same organization may therefore be exceptional at mobilization and routine repetition yet progressively worse at search, novelty, and adaptation.

The argument separates the right to decide from responsibility for consequences. It shows why accumulated buffers can hide an ongoing transition for years: observed output—and at the macro level even GDP—may continue to grow by inertia while fewer new economic cycles are initiated. Local failures may become less frequent while the cost of a rare common failure rises.

The Soviet experience illustrates both sides of the curve: extraordinary coordination in war, reconstruction, industrial development, and scientific missions, followed by a bureaucratic plateau in which procedure increasingly replaced responsibility for outcomes. China after 1978 provides a contrasting movement—not from state to pure market, but toward bounded spaces in which local actors could again choose more of a trajectory and retain more of its consequences.

The practical criterion is precise: effective consolidation ends where the next unit of coordination destroys more self-directed local Action than it saves in coordination cost. That is where coordination begins to turn into hypercontrol.

This working paper is part of the AFG Research Series and develops the MICRO-level analysis of Action, Decision Sovereignty, Consequence Responsibility, consolidation, and the nonlinear organizational cost of coordination.

title: Calibration and skill of archived real-time SARS-CoV-2 variant forecasts

detail.title: Calibration and skill of archived real-time SARS-CoV-2 variant forecasts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Since December 2022 the Nextstrain project has published daily probabilistic forecasts of SARS-CoV-2 variant frequencies with 50%, 80% and 95% credible intervals, leaving 770 timestamped, immutable snapshots. Published evaluations refit these models to reconstructed data. We evaluate the forecasts as they were issued. Doing so first requires removing a structural obstacle: the clade partition is redefined every three to five weeks, faster than frequencies settle, so matching a forecast to an outcome by label compares different quantities. We introduce partition-matched scoring, which compares like with like, and quantify the trade-off it creates between letting observations settle and holding the partition fixed. On 117,438 matched pairs from 55 forecast dates, the forecasts improve on a naive baseline by 32.6% in mean absolute error, yet their intervals are too narrow: a stated 95% interval covers 34.1%. A weighted-interval-score decomposition attributes 46% of the score to miscalibration, and out-of-time conformal recalibration restores near-nominal coverage. Both results hold on a second data branch, and the coverage shortfall also appears in influenza forecasts from the same pipeline.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare.

detail.abstract: Postnatal care provided by medical professional is necessary for lowering maternal deaths that is prevalent in developing countries like India. Using the NFHS-5/DHS (2019-21), India's nationally representative household survey data, we apply three machine-learning models-LASSO, Random Forest and XGBoost-to predict whether mothers receive postnatal care. Tree-based ensembles outperform LASSO; XGBoost appears to o er the best balance between precision and recall, while Random Forest generates highest recall. Feature-importance analyses across models converge on six critical factors that are related to antenatal-care intensity, institutional delivery, informational outreach, religion, health-insurance coverage and state of residence. These results highlight persistent socioeconomic and informational barriers that targeted policies could address. Our approach demonstrates how machine-learning tools can guide resource-constrained health systems by predicting under-served mothers.

detail.abstract: On a panel of 37.2 million observations from voter rolls, deeds, and permits, Republicans install solar panels less often than Democrats in the same ZIP and year, by 17 to 23 percent of the unconditional adoption rate. The gap is several times larger on permits pulled in the household's own name than on homes that came with panels, is cut by two thirds for absentee owners and is present among renters. It does not widen where the grid produces more carbon emissions and varies little with the retail electricity rate. These results suggest that the gap is primarily driven by the social image motive, rather than by pecuniary returns and environmental impact.

title: CCSI03, Poverty Reduction, and Human Welfare: A Citizen-Centered Framework for Diagnosing Multidimensional Poverty and Transforming Economic Resources into Welfare

detail.title: CCSI03, Poverty Reduction, and Human Welfare: A Citizen-Centered Framework for Diagnosing Multidimensional Poverty and Transforming Economic Resources into Welfare

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal, financial, or other relationships that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because the study uses secondary, publicly available aggregate data and does not involve human participants or identifiable personal data.

detail.abstract: Poverty is commonly evaluated through monetary measures of income or consumption, yet deprivation also reflects limited access to education, health, essential services, institutional quality, social inclusion, security, and other dimensions of human well-being. This paper develops the Citizen-Centered Strategic Index (CCSI03) as a multidimensional framework for analyzing how economic, institutional, and social resources may be transformed into improved human welfare and, potentially, reduced poverty. CCSI03 integrates five conceptual dimensions: Economic and Welfare Environment (EWE), Human Development Capacity (HDC), Institutional Governance Quality (IGQ), Social Sustainability and Inclusion (SSI), and Stability and Fundamental Security (SFS). The framework shifts analytical attention from the volume of economic resources toward the effectiveness with which those resources may be translated into citizen welfare. The paper distinguishes poverty measurement from the mechanisms that may influence poverty reduction. CCSI03 is therefore not proposed as a replacement for established monetary or multidimensional poverty measures. Instead, it is proposed as a complementary diagnostic and policy framework for identifying potential constraints in the conversion of economic resources into welfare outcomes. The paper develops a formal index structure, theoretical propositions, testable hypotheses, a variable-measurement matrix, and an empirical strategy based on panel-data methods. Preliminary empirical analysis associated with the broader CCSI03 research program indicates a positive relationship between CCSI03 and real household consumption per capita under fixed-effects specifications. These estimates are interpreted as preliminary associations rather than causal evidence and do not constitute a completed test of the effect of CCSI03 on poverty. The central contribution is methodological and analytical: CCSI03 provides a citizen-centered framework through which poverty can be studied not only as a shortage of income but also as a problem of incomplete conversion of available resources into sustainable human welfare. Further empirical research is required to determine whether higher CCSI03 values are systematically associated with lower poverty and whether such relationships are causal.

detail.abstract: Planetary Communitarianism and the Limits of WTO Governance: Agriculture as a Diagnostic Lens for Justice and Survivability. Global trade governance increasingly confronts stresses arising from ecological degradation, systemic inequality, and geopolitical fragmentation. Yet prevailing liberal justice theories such as cosmopolitan, liberal-egalitarian, and libertarian approaches remain insu iciently attentive to irreversible harm. This paper proposes planetary communitarianism as a conceptual framework that complements existing approaches by foregrounding responsibility, interdependence, and the conditions required for the long-term functioning of human governance systems. The paper draws on the metaphysics of Spinozistic conatus and a precautionary orientation without creating a conflict between human and non-human claims. WTO governance of agriculture is employed as a critical case study to demonstrate these justice tensions and reveal their structural origins. Water scarcity, pesticide externalities, soil degradation, monocultures, financialisation, and concentrated agri-corporate power illustrate how extractive agricultural systems depend on allocation patterns that are fundamentally misaligned with ecological limits. Within the WTO framework the Agreement on Agriculture (AoA), the Sanitary and Phytosanitary Agreement (SPS), and the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) expose systemic asymmetries between developed and developing countries and highlight the limited capacity of existing trade rules to incorporate intergenerational, distributive, and ecological justice considerations. Together, these agreements form a triad that normalises and stabilises industrial agricultural systems while remaining neither su iciently aligned with nor meaningfully coordinated with Earth system boundaries.

title: Creators Have Difficulty Abandoning Ideas They Generated
affiliations: and University of Toronto

detail.title: Creators Have Difficulty Abandoning Ideas They Generated

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We have no conflicts of interest to disclose.
declarations.funderStatement: We received no specific funding for this work.

detail.abstract: Creativity researchers often distinguish between two stages of the creative process: generation versus selection. While much is known about the psychology of idea generation (e.g., the factors that lead to a greater number of novel and useful ideas), less is understood about the nature of selection, or how generation and selection interact. Here we investigate how the act of generating ideas may potentially distort the selection process. Using an incentive-compatible paradigm in which pairs of participants reviewed the same ideas and were rewarded for submitting only highquality ideas, we find that people submit a greater number of lower-quality ideas when selecting among their own ideas than when selecting among another person's ideas (the Creative Endowment Effect). This effect generalizes across three tasks in two domains and is resistant to an informational intervention (i.e., explicitly telling people about the effect). However, having participants revisit their ideas several months later increases their selectivity. The broader implications for individuals and organizations are discussed.

title: Measurement Without Structure: The Drift of Econometrics from Unification to Parameter Testing
affiliations: Nguyen Tat Thanh University

detail.title: Measurement Without Structure: The Drift of Econometrics from Unification to Parameter Testing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Econometrics was founded as the unification of economic theory, statistics and mathematics, with the explicit claim that none of the three alone constitutes the discipline. Nine decades later, its dominant empirical practice is the estimation of a reduced-form coefficient followed by a test of a hypothesis about its value, from which economic meaning is then inferred. This review traces how that drift occurred and argues that it has left four objects of every regression-the slope, the intercept, the residual and the diagnosis of endogeneity-without determinate economic content. Beginning with the invention of least squares by Legendre and Gauss as a method of averaging, the paper shows that ordinary least squares returns the best linear approximation to a conditional expectation, and that the data are silent on what ought to condition on what. It then follows the founding programme through Frisch, Haavelmo and the Cowles-NBER dispute to the present practice of parameter testing, and documents four literatures in which the resulting confusion has already been diagnosed independently: aggregate production functions, complete demand systems, financial statement data, and tests of the capital asset pricing model. These are argued to be four expressions of a single proposition: the statistical identity of a parameter does not determine its economic identity. The paper closes by proposing that econometrics be repositioned as economic measurement, governed by a taxonomy of six kinds of economic relation and six questions to be settled before estimation rather than after it. Statistical adequacy and structural specification are treated throughout as separate and equally necessary requirements, neither substituting for the other. The contribution is conceptual and methodological; no new estimator is proposed.

detail.abstract: Evaluations of public support to firms measure research spending, patenting and employment, and take registry status as the treatment. Contributions to operating income are filed in every Italian statutory account and are non-zero in 41.7 per cent of them. Using 62,214 firm-year observations on 9,679 unlisted firms over 2015-2024-innovative start-ups, innovative SMEs and ordinary SMEs drawn from one source on identical items-we place the transfer beside the firm's own cash flow in a within-firm investment equation. Additionality is partial: full additionality and full substitution are both rejected. The effect is intensive rather than extensive, an indicator for receiving anything carrying-0.006 against 0.376 for the amount. Fungibility is rejected in ratio form and cannot be rejected once no scaling is imposed on either side, at 0.121 against 0.153. A taxonomy estimated without the outcome reproduces the regulatory gradient, and flexible learners improve on the linear form by 1.26 times.

title: The Half-Billion-Dollar Gift An Examination of the Department of Defense SkillBridge Program Through the Definitional Framework of Corporate Welfare

detail.abstract: The Department of Defense (War) SkillBridge program permits transitioning service members to perform up to 180 days of work for private-sector hosts while remaining on full military compensation, at no cost to the host organization. Although the program is uniformly described in policy discourse as a benefit to service members, no prior study has examined its structure from the perspective of the firms that receive its central input: government-funded labor. This study applied the definitional framework of corporate welfare, synthesized from the public-choice, economic-development-incentive, tax-expenditure, and submerged-state literatures, to the SkillBridge program as it operates in practice. Using a documentary audit methodology — a multi-filter export and deduplication of the program's public directory yielding a union corpus of 4,255 unique programs across 2,732 organizations (with a replicated state-anchored census of 1,527 programs and 1,103 organizations retained for comparison), a live-requisition verification pilot, contractual analysis of the August 2024 Memorandum of Understanding, mechanical extraction of 640 binding requirements from six governing issuances, and a scenario-bounded valuation of the labor transfer — the study tested whether the program satisfies three definitional criteria: transfer of value to particular firms, particularity in the direction of that benefit, and absence of verified conditionality. Findings indicate that all three criteria are satisfied: the program transfers an estimated half a billion dollars per year in taxpayer-funded labor to private hosts — $316–732 million (central ≈ $506M) in FY2024 dollars and $308–703 million (central ≈ $490M) in FY2026 dollars, a robustness result in which lower participation against higher unit compensation returns approximately the same total under both vintages; the benefit is particular by design and direction rather than by firm-level capture — the program imposes no per-firm ceiling, no aggregate budget, and no allocation mechanism; 52.2% of programs carry the self-attested defense-industrial-base designation that a June 2026 Secretary-level instrument converts into a presumption of approval (a field validated by no instrument, and internally inconsistent for 29.4% of organizations operating more than one program); and the organizations operating the most programs are drawn disproportionately from government agencies and staffing intermediaries, the two host populations to which the program's sole outcome warranty least applies; and every conditioning mechanism present in the program's governing instruments is either unenforced or unverifiable, with no sourced outcome dataset located in the audit's finite search (the sole published figure is an unsourced budget-justification assertion). The study concludes that SkillBridge, as currently governed, constitutes an in-kind, submerged, unconditioned labor subsidy — a category the literature associates with windfall effects the audit independently observed — and that a defined set of conditionality reforms would convert the subsidy into a performance-verified workforce investment without altering the program's statutory design.

title: Zero Trust at the Seams: Architecture, Interoperability, and Governance Challenges in Federal Shared Services

detail.title: Zero Trust at the Seams: Architecture, Interoperability, and Governance Challenges in Federal Shared Services

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare that I have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: To the authors' knowledge, this is the first paper to frame federal shared-services interoperability the Quality Service Management Office (QSMO) marketplace model as a documented, high-stakes instance of the multi-domain, federated zero trust problem that recent systematic reviews identify as underexamined in the broader literature. Executive Order 14028 and OMB Memorandum M-22-09 direct federal civilian agencies to implement Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) against an implicit model of a single, administratively bounded enterprise. Under the QSMO shared-services model, however, agencies increasingly consume financial management, cybersecurity, grants management, and human capital services from marketplaces operated by other agencies, extending the zero-trust boundary across an organizational seam that neither NIST SP 800-207 nor the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model was designed to address. This paper surveys the technical, governance, and equity implications of that seam. It reviews the identity-centric, multi-cloud, and federatedidentity mechanisms including NIST SP 800-207A and emerging IETF WIMSE workload-identity federation that are candidates for bridging independently administered trust domains; documents, through federal audit findings, the legacy-system incompatibility and inconsistent identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) practices that currently prevent interoperable zero trust from being realized in QSMO marketplaces; and examines the Department of Homeland Security's multi-year, still-incomplete effort to federate zero trust across its own components as a documented analogue for the harder problem of federating zero trust across independent cabinet agencies. The paper concludes with a governance and standards agenda a shared ICAM profile across QSMOs, mandated federation protocols, and machine-readable, continuously verified compliance data for closing the gap between the federal zero trust mandate and the federal shared-services mandate.

title: The Alan Turing–Pet Shop Boys Paradox: Artificial Intelligence, Digital Identity and the Legal Construction of the Human Self

detail.title: The Alan Turing–Pet Shop Boys Paradox: Artificial Intelligence, Digital Identity and the Legal Construction of the Human Self

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. During the preparation of this manuscript, AI-based language and research-assistance tools were used for drafting support, research organization, literature discovery, analytical structuring, and language refinement; the author critically reviewed, edited, verified, and assumed full responsibility for all legal analysis and conclusions.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Legal regimes built to protect identity against artificial intelligence — voice-misappropriation torts, the German general personality right, Denmark's 2025–2026 copyright-based likeness right, and the disclosure duties of Article 50 of the EU AI Act — share a common structural premise inherited from Alan Turing's 1950 imitation game: that identity is legally cognizable through behavioral indistinguishability, and that the wrong worth remedying occurs when a synthetic performance is mistaken for an authentic human origin. This premise supplies a coherent test for voice-cloning and deepfake harms, but it supplies no doctrinal vocabulary for the inverse and increasingly commercially significant phenomenon in which a human performer constructs legal and artistic selfhood by deliberately adopting machine-coded affect — deadpan delivery, synthesized timbre, mechanized visual iconography — without any intent to deceive as to origin. Using the sustained aesthetic practice of the recording duo Pet Shop Boys as an illustrative case of authorship built on performed machine-likeness, this article argues that contemporary identity-protection doctrine exhibits a directional asymmetry: it defines the protected interest by proximity to unmediated biological origin, leaving those whose recognizable selfhood is constituted by anti-naturalistic performance systematically underprotected precisely where their imitation is most successful. Employing comparative doctrinal analysis across the United States, Germany, Denmark, the European Union, the United Kingdom, and Brazil, the article traces this asymmetry through voice-misappropriation case law, personality-right jurisprudence, and the new generation of deepfake statutes, and proposes a Reciprocal Identity Attribution Standard that severs legal protection from the assumption of naturalistic origin without weakening anti-deepfake enforcement. The analysis contributes a doctrinal distinction — between origin-deception harms and persona-displacement harms — that existing frameworks do not draw, and identifies the conditions under which each applies.

title: Which Constraint Binds First? Computation, Data Regimes and Institutional Absorption in Emerging-Market Financial Analytics

detail.title: Which Constraint Binds First? Computation, Data Regimes and Institutional Absorption in Emerging-Market Financial Analytics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual paper involving no human participants, no patients and no personal data. No new data were generated or analysed.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funding from any agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Purpose — Advanced analytics has entered emerging-market financial institutions through a vocabulary
borrowed from advanced economies, in which computational capacity is treated as the scarce input. This
paper asks which constraint actually binds first — computational access, data-regime depth, or institutional
absorption — and what follows for method selection and investment sequencing.
Design/methodology/approach — Conceptual paper. Three literatures are combined: the resource-based
and dynamic-capabilities account of analytics capability, the institutional-voids account of emerging
markets, and the financial machine-learning literature on estimator requirements. A three-layer constraint-
ordering framework is constructed with observable indicators for each layer, and six propositions are
derived, each paired with the evidence that would refute it.
Findings — Computational capacity, being rentable, divisible and globally priced, rarely satisfies rarity or
inimitability and so rarely binds. The data regime binds more often, through short panels, thin cross-sections
and unlinked records. Where compute and data are both adequate, output is capped by absorption: model-
risk governance, supervisory acceptance and the authority to act on a model output. Method transferability
is conditional rather than general.
Originality/value — The analytics-capability literature bundles hardware and data into one technical-
resource construct. Separating them yields a diagnostic that locates the marginal return to analytics
investment and predicts a specific failure mode: measurable capability accompanied by no measurable
change in decisions.
Research limitations/implications — The framework is untested. Its indicators are proposed rather than
validated, and the layers may be less separable in practice than in construction, particularly where data and
talent constraints move together.
Practical implications — Boards and supervisors can sequence analytics investment against a diagnosed
constraint rather than a technology roadmap, and can put one question to any analytics proposal: which layer
does this loosen?
Social implications — Where the binding constraint is institutional rather than technical, expanding
compute will not extend credit to thin-file borrowers, and inclusion targets tied to technology procurement
will be missed.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impacts of Mercosur on Brazilian local labor markets. We find that the preferential tariff reductions implemented by Argentina, Paraguay, and Uruguay led to a significant increase in formal employment in Brazil's most exposed regions relative to less exposed ones. Furthermore, given that Brazilian unilateral trade liberalization coincided with the establishment of Mercosur, we investigate whether previous estimates of the effects of unilateral liberalization hold when accounting for Mercosur tariff reductions. Our findings indicate that the negative employment effects of unilateral liberalization approximately double when controlling for Mercosur, suggesting that previous studies underestimate the impact by omitting the offsetting export demand stimulus from the preferential agreement. We also find suggestive evidence of positive effects on regional earnings premia, reported in an appendix.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how loan officer industry specialization shapes corporate loan pricing and contract design. Using hand-collected data linking individual officers to large corporate loans from 1995-2023, I show that more specialized officers at the same bank, lending to the same borrower, charge lower interest spreads after controlling for relationship lending and bank-level specialization. A Bartik-style instrument based on national industry credit growth mitigates endogeneity concerns. Pricing gains are concentrated among informationally opaque borrowers. Beyond pricing, specialized officers also write more flexible, customized contracts without altering borrowers' ex post performance. Overall, industry-specific expertise at the officer level ameliorates information frictions and improves contractual efficiency.

detail.abstract: Each year the United States returns between 148,315 and roughly 200,000 service members to civilian life — the federal sources disagree by 26% and none reconciles them — through an ecosystem Congress has legislated and funded piece by piece: a mandated occupational crosswalk to translate military skills, a credentialing apparatus, an internship marketplace (SkillBridge), and a mandatory transition curriculum (the Transition Assistance Program). The Government Accountability Office has reported on this ecosystem at least ten times in nine years and has verified almost none of it. This audit does, using only public data, the government's own binding instructions, and receipt-grade evidence: every figure traces to a committed source file or a cited public record, and the correction log is published with the paper. The crosswalk members are told to trust was last quality-reviewed in 2014; of 48,042 Air Force specialty-to-occupation links, 0.51% have ever been human-reviewed, and a systematic comparison of every specialty's published training standard against every civilian occupation's task statements finds the median offered occupation ranks 75th of 922 on task similarity, with 42.6% outside the top 100 and 90.9% of offers identical across skill levels. The SkillBridge marketplace advertises 11,532 positions behind which no enumeration exists; its own export instrument cannot produce one. Since August 2024, every provider warrants a 75% qualifying-offer rate that no federal dataset can verify, while members on full military pay supply an estimated $316–732 million per year of labor, for up to 180 days each, to hosts who pay nothing. Access collapses by rank and branch even as it goes unverified, and the market follows employer demand rather than member need. The audit closes with the Freedom of Information Act requests, correction requests, and statutory changes that would make each layer verifiable.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between auditor choice, ownership, transparency & disclosure (T&D) and corporate governance compliance (CGC) in 52 Istanbul Stock Exchange firms. We collect ownership data from the annual reports, measure T&D in collaboration with Standard & Poor’s and compliance with local CG Principles by evaluating the Compliance Reports. We associate the auditor selection decision with the T&D and CGC scores while controlling for common determinants of auditor choice. We also test whether the T&D and CGC scores are predictors of the type of opinion rendered. detail.abstract: This paper presents a comparative legal analysis of the immigration systems of four major Western nations: Canada, Germany, the United States, and the United Kingdom. Recognizing that immigration policy is a critical nexus of national sovereignty, economic necessity, and humanitarian obligation, this study examines the distinct legal frameworks, policy objectives, and administrative mechanisms that define each country's approach. The analysis is structured around four core pillars: (1) the legal pathways for economic and skilled migration, (2) the frameworks for family reunification, (3) the regimes for asylum and refugee protection, and (4) the systems for enforcement, including detention and deportation. Through a doctrinal and comparative legal methodology, the paper identifies key convergences, such as a shared shift towards points-based systems and a tightening of asylum procedures, alongside profound divergences rooted in each nation's unique constitutional traditions, federal structures, and political landscapes. The findings reveal that while Canada and Germany exhibit more flexible and federally coordinated models that facilitate integration, the US and UK systems are increasingly characterized by legislative volatility, judicial contestation, and administrative complexity, leading to significant backlogs and uncertainty. Ultimately, this analysis argues that the effectiveness of an immigration system is not solely determined by its stated policies but by the coherence between its legal architecture, administrative capacity, and underlying political consensus. The paper concludes by offering comparative insights that can inform policy reform and legal scholarship on managing migration in an era of global flux.

detail.abstract:
India's emergence as a significant defence manufacturing economy has increased the strategic importance of the industrial systems that support the production, movement and sustainment of defence equipment. Policy discussions concerning defence self-reliance have traditionally concentrated on procurement, technology development, manufacturing capacity and indigenisation. Comparatively less attention has been given to the transport and logistics infrastructure required to connect geographically dispersed production centres, suppliers, research institutions and markets. This paper examines the potential role of Indian Railways as a component of India's strategic industrial infrastructure and evaluates its relevance to the country's expanding defence manufacturing ecosystem. The study employs an exploratory qualitative research design based on secondary data analysis, policy review and a case-study approach. It examines official data relating to defence production, defence exports, railway freight performance, Dedicated Freight Corridors (DFCs) and industrial-corridor development. Particular attention is given to the Uttar Pradesh Defence Industrial Corridor (UPDIC), which provides an illustrative case of a geographically distributed defence-industrial ecosystem situated within a rapidly evolving multimodal infrastructure environment. The findings suggest that the strategic value of railway infrastructure for defence manufacturing lies not simply in the transportation of finished military equipment. Its more significant contribution may lie in enabling the movement of raw materials, heavy engineering inputs, intermediate components and capital equipment across geographically dispersed production networks. The growing capacity of Indian Railways, the expansion of dedicated freight infrastructure and the development of industrial corridors create opportunities for greater integration between national logistics planning and defenceindustrial policy.
However, the study also finds that the existence of large-scale railway infrastructure alone does not automatically generate defence-industrial competitiveness. Realising this potential requires deliberate integration of rail terminals, industrial sidings, warehousing, multimodal logistics facilities, specialised handling systems and digital supply-chain networks. The paper concludes that railway planning should be increasingly considered within India's broader framework of strategic industrial resilience and recommends a formal mechanism for integrating defence-industrial clusters with national logistics infrastructure.

detail.title: Capital Heterogeneity, Shadow Credit, and Asymmetric Liquidation: Malinvestment in the Generative AI Infrastructure Boom

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of Generative AI (GenAI) infrastructure investment between 2023 and 2026 coincided with a severe contraction in commodity memory (DRAM) supply and a sharp rise in consumer hardware prices. Applying Austrian Capital Theory and an institutionally bounded extension of Austrian Business Cycle Theory (ABCT), this paper argues that the episode reflects genuine capital malinvestment rather than a transitory supply bottleneck: reallocating scarce 300mm silicon-wafer capacity toward High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) is an unsustainable elongation of the structure of production. Because this boom occurred under a historically restrictive Federal Reserve policy rate, we decompose its financing into three tiers – an antecedent 2020–2022 monetary expansion that capitalized corporate and private-credit reserves, non-monetary federal semiconductor subsidy, and duration-transforming GPU-collateralized shadow credit – and state, tier by tier, the evidence that would falsify each. Grounding the analysis in the physical constraints of sub-micron 3D packaging, we show that the specialized equipment behind this reallocation is functionally non-convertible to commodity memory production even once its acquisition cost is written off in bankruptcy, though we bound this liquidation problem to its actual, modest share of aggregate AI infrastructure capital rather than letting it imply a macroeconomic weight the underlying capital layer does not carry. We reconcile the rapid 24–36 month obsolescence of AI-specific hardware with a slower, multi-year recovery of commodity memory supply, and bound all empirical claims to the memory and advanced-packaging segment of the 2023–2026 cycle.
