detail.abstract: About a third of all food produced is lost or wasted; reducing that share is the object of Sustainable Development Goal 12.3. This study asks whether machine learning can predict food loss from the attributes recorded in the UN Food Loss and Waste Database-country, commodity, supply chain stage and year-and under what evaluation it holds. Eight regression models were fitted to 26,970 records across 159 countries and tested two ways: training on years up to each of five cutoffs from 2016-2020, and holding out entire country and commodity pairs. Both were scored against persistence and linear-trend baselines with paired bootstrap confidence intervals. The results separate two capabilities usually reported together. On magnitude, no model consistently improves on repeating a group's last recorded value, and predictions understate severe losses, averaging 13.2% where observations exceed 20% against a true mean of 29.6%. On ordering, the random forest reaches an average precision of 0.434 against the baseline's 0.333 at every cutoff, and its highest-ranked 5% of records contains 41.5% of all severe losses, 8.3 times the rate of an unranked sample. The advantage is largest where no measurement exists: on held-out pairs error falls to 2.51 against 3.69. This matters because of what the database lacks: of 1,437 country and commodity pairs, 853 are measured at a single stage and 9,651 plausible combinations have none. Such models are best understood not as replacements for measurement but as a means of directing it: screening instruments, not sources of severity estimates.

title: Macroeconomic Implications of Permit Market: Evidence from India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme
affiliations: , Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research and Reserve Bank of India

detail.title: Macroeconomic Implications of Permit Market: Evidence from India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme
detail.abstract: We study how a carbon permit market shapes firm-level emission reduction incentives and aggregate environmental and macroeconomic outcomes. We develop a novel and tractable microeconomic framework in which firms endogenously decide whether to become a permit seller. We find that a higher previous period abatement or current green energy adoption increases a firm's probability of becoming a permit seller but reduces equilibrium share of permit sellers as overall compliance improves, revealing a distinction between individual and aggregate participation. We embed this mechanism in an Environmental-Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium model of India's emission intensity target policy. We find that it achieves energy transition at lower economic costs than a carbon tax. A stricter target and cheaper green energy can accelerate this transition. Finally, endogenous permit price adjustment accommodates shocks that increase fossil-fuel dependence from translating into higher fossil-fuel use, providing a novel stabilization mechanism for permit markets.

title: Adoption of Improved Soybean Varieties and Its Impact on Households’ Food Security: The Case of Pawe Woreda, Western Ethiopia
affiliations: , Bahir Dar University and International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) and Bahirdar University

detail.title: Adoption of Improved Soybean Varieties and Its Impact on Households’ Food Security: The Case of Pawe Woreda, Western Ethiopia
detail.abstract: The importance of agricultural technology in enhancing the welfares of farmers can be realized when yield gain from the technologies results in meaningful gain in nutritionally adequate foods. In this regard, improved varieties were play a great role in improving households food security, food consumption, and food diversity, and there-by contributing to nutrition security. This study therefore, analyzed factors that influence adoption of improved soybean varieties and its effect on households’ food security. The study was conducted in Pawe district. Hurdle models were used to analyze factors affecting adoption and intensity of improved soybean varieties. An endogenous switching regression (ESR) model was used to analyze the impact of improved soybean varieties on households’ food security – i.e. using food security scale, food consumption score, and household dietary diversity score as proxy variables. The double Hurdle models results showed that family size, Farm Size, the existence of neighbor adopters, market distance, extension credit, perception, training, and total household income were the driving factors of adoption probability and use intensity of improved soybean varieties. The ESR model results indicated that adoption of improved soybean varieties increases the average dietary diversity score and food consumption scale by 0.53 and 5.91 points, respectively. Consistently, the food security scale estimation result also showed that adoption of improved soybean varieties reduces food insecurity by 2.56 units. These results suggest that promotion and adoption of improved soybean varieties will contribute to improve the nutritional status of the farming households.

title: Bad Care
affiliations: University of Cambridge - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Bad Care

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A

detail.abstract: Feminist criticisms of the ethics of care-from both within and outside the approach's own fold-have historically charged care ethics with "valorising caring". Feminist care ethicists have responded to this criticism by acknowledging that care can sometimes be bad-it can be performed poorly, prove lacking or deficient in some respect, or take place under deeply unjust structural conditions. But this consensus leaves the harder and more important question untouched-and it is this question that explains why the criticisms persist. Can caring actions be bad insofar as they are caring? Can the very feature that makes an action caring also make it morally bad? I argue here that it can. Analysing a range of caring actions that strike us as bad, I identify one category-which I call 'true bad care'wherein the very feature that makes the act caring is also what makes it morally bad. Here, the badness stems from the agent's intention to fulfil another's needs-one characterised by a paternalistic disregard for the recipient's say. Since such cases of true bad care exist, caring actions are not necessarily valuable even insofar as they are caring. This finding clarifies the moral valence of care ethics' foundational concept and paves the way for further development of the approach along these revised lines. It also demonstrates that paternalism and care are more conceptually intertwined than philosophers acknowledge. Paternalistic actions are not separate from care. They are the central case of bad care.

detail.abstract:
Background: Preoperative assessment of adult-type diffuse gliomas involves evaluation of tumor extent, integrated histomolecular diagnosis, CNS WHO grade, and prognosis. Although deep learning has been increasingly applied to individual imaging tasks, most studies have focused on these tasks separately rather than addressing them within a common framework.

Purpose: To develop and externally validate a three-dimensional multitask learning framework using routine multimodal MRI for tumor subregion segmentation, integrated diagnostic category prediction, CNS WHO grade classification, and survival risk stratification in adult-type diffuse gliomas.

Materials and Methods: In this retrospective multicenter study, 1,982 adults with histopathologically confirmed glioma were included from three clinical institutions and four publicly available datasets. Preoperative T1-weighted, contrast-enhanced T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images were used as model inputs. A three-dimensional end-to-end network, termed Tumor Multitask Transformer U-Net (TMTR), was developed using 1,015 patients from the UPenn-GBM and UCSF-PDGM datasets, which were randomly split into training, validation, and internal test sets at a ratio of 8:1:1. Five independent cohorts were used for external evaluation. TMTR was trained to segment tumor subregions and predict integrated diagnostic categories, CNS WHO grade, and survival risk. Segmentation performance was assessed using Dice scores and boundary-based metrics, diagnostic performance using accuracy, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, and F1 score, and prognostic performance using Kaplan–Meier analysis and log-rank tests. 

Results: Among 1,982 adults with diffuse glioma included from seven data sources, median age across cohorts ranged from 42.5 to 62.7 years, and the study population covered CNS WHO grades 2–4 and the major adult-type diffuse glioma categories, including glioblastoma, oligodendroglioma, and IDH-mutant astrocytoma. In the internal test set, TMTR achieved mean Dice scores of 0.94 ± 0.05 for whole tumor, 0.95 ± 0.04 for necrotic/non-enhancing tumor, 0.96 ± 0.03 for peritumoral edema, and 0.91 ± 0.13 for enhancing tumor. Across external cohorts, whole-tumor Dice scores ranged from 0.87 to 0.94, and edema Dice scores were at least 0.95. For integrated diagnostic classification, internal test accuracy and AUC were 0.99 and 1.00, respectively, while recall for GBM ranged from 0.96 to 1.00 across external cohorts. For CNS WHO grade prediction, internal test accuracy and AUC were 0.988 and 0.997, respectively. Across external cohorts, accuracy ranged from 0.860 to 0.940 and AUC from 0.972 to 0.989; recall for CNS WHO grade 4 tumors ranged from 0.985 to 1.000. The imaging-derived risk score significantly stratified overall survival in the training cohort and in the Beijing Tiantan Hospital, Shache County People’s Hospital, and TCGA cohorts (all P<0.05).

Conclusion: A three-dimensional multitask model using routine preoperative multimodal MRI provided accurate tumor segmentation and prediction of integrated diagnostic categories and CNS WHO grade across multiple cohorts. title: Industry Context vs. Career Mindsets: A Cross-Sectional Path Analysis of Multi-Dimensional Organizational Commitment in Fractional Executives

detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationships between industry context, career orientation and organizational commitment of 170 fractional C-Suite executives. Utilizing a cross-sectional quantitative design in seven distinct industry sectors, analysis of variance was combined with exploratory path modeling to evaluate operating context as both a categorical grouping variable and a structural mediator that was operationalized via industry agility. One-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) results reveal that fractional executives maintain consistently high, statistically uniform protean and boundaryless career orientations across all industry sectors, positioning these mindsets as baseline behavioral characteristics of the fractional model rather than sector-driven outcomes. However, significant industry-driven variations emerged for overall organizational commitment, and normative commitment, with dynamic sectors like technology and finance generating higher commitment baselines than traditional fields like healthcare and education. Path modeling rejected mediation due to a non-significant relationship between career orientation and industry. Instead, the structural models uncovered a condition where personal career orientation and high-agility industrial environments independently drive overall loyalty. Furthermore, the model demonstrates environmental predominance over individual differences, as high-agility sector context acts as an attachment inducer that directly generates normative commitment while rendering individual protean mindsets non-significant. These findings imply that while fractional leaders carry a self-directed career orientation everywhere, their structural integration is heavily governed by sector-specific agility. Organizations must consequently look past cultural onboarding and focus instead on stripping away bureaucratic bottlenecks to unlock fractional executive's performance and loyalty.

title: Pricing the Road Ahead -Urban Road Pricing in Developing-Country Cities
affiliations: University of Melbourne

detail.title: Pricing the Road Ahead -Urban Road Pricing in Developing-Country Cities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest

detail.abstract: Urban road pricing is among the most theoretically robust instruments in transport economics. Its promise-internalising congestion, risk and pollution externalities, generating dedicated revenue for public transport, and reshaping motorisation trajectories-maps with acute precision onto the urban mobility conditions prevailing in developing-country cities. Yet every implemented urban road pricing scheme in the world operates in a high-income city: Singapore, Stockholm, London, Gothenburg, Milan, and New York. This paper examines that paradox and develops a prescriptive framework to resolve it. The central argument is that the non-adoption of road pricing in developing-country cities is not an accident of policy indifference but a product of identifiable institutional, fiscal, political, and technical barriers that have a discoverable structure. Drawing on urban transport theory, institutional economics, and governance literature (Gwilliam, 2003; Gakenheimer, 1999; Santos, 2004; Small & Verhoef, 2007), this paper introduces the concept of the feasibility frontier-the minimum viable combination of conditions required for road pricing to be implementable-and proposes three distinct policy pathways through which cities at different positions relative to that frontier can sequence their way toward implementation. The framework is illustrated through brief applications to Bogotá, Nairobi, and Jakarta. The central normative claim is that the cities most in need of road pricing are fully capable of implementing it, but doing so requires abandoning the sequencing logic inherited from high-income cities-which builds public transport before pricing roads-in favour of an inverse logic that uses pricing revenue as the mechanism to fund the public transport that does not yet exist.

title: Forecast-relevant Information in Supply Networks: The Case of Cash Flow Forecasting
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School and Emory University - Goizueta Business School

detail.title: Forecast-relevant Information in Supply Networks: The Case of Cash Flow Forecasting

detail.abstract: Problem Definition: Operating cash flow constrains a firm's ability to fund procurement, production, and shortterm responses to shocks. Firms therefore plan their operations around expectations of near-term cash flows, and shortfalls relative to those expectations trigger costly adjustments. However, it is difficult to forecast cash flows because receipts and payments depend partly on customers and suppliers. In this paper, we ask whether information from a firm's observed supply network improves one-quarter-ahead cash-flow forecasts and, more importantly, how that forecast-relevant information is distributed over the network. Methodology/results: To do so, we combine FactSet Revere supplier-customer relationship data with Compustat fundamentals for 3,816 firms from 2011Q1-2023Q4 and train a graph attention network (GAT) to predict cash inflows and outflows in a rolling window design. GAT allows partner information to enter each forecast through relationship-specific weights, which we use to define the edge-gradient sensitivity, a measure that ranks each relationship by its contribution to the forecast. We find that GAT delivers lower mean absolute percentage error than a broad set of linear, regularized, nonlinear, and neighbor-average-augmented benchmarks, establishing that supply network information is valuable beyond focal-firm histories and coarse network averages. This information is highly concentrated: the top 20% of relationships by edge-gradient sensitivity account for roughly 90% of forecast-relevant information, and removing the bottom 70% of edges leaves average forecast accuracy essentially unchanged. Importantly, the resulting core subnetwork is stable across forecast epochs. We further find that re-estimating the model on the core subnetwork can improve out-of-sample accuracy relative to the full graph. Managerial implications: Using Walmart as a case study, we show how the framework recovers the forecast-relevant core subnetwork for an individual firm. Our concentration result has a direct implication for the costly problem of supply-chain visibility. When a firm can monitor only the top K of its observed partners, edge-gradient sensitivity selects more forecast-relevant relationships than rankings based on observed firm characteristics. The framework therefore offers a screening device for prioritizing partner monitoring, information acquisition, and network stress-testing efforts.

detail.abstract: This study examines how CEOs with lobbying experience influence corporate innovation, climate-related strategies, investment decisions, and firm performance. I document substantial differences across industries. In non-high-tech sectors, lobbyist CEOs are associated with lower patenting activity, fewer green patents, reduced climate-related engagement, and a greater emphasis on capital expenditures rather than R&D. In contrast, firms led by lobbyist CEOs in high-tech industries produce significantly more patents and green patents, generate higher-value innovations, and invest more heavily in R&D. I also find that lobbyist CEOs are associated with lower climate change exposure and reduced discussion of climaterelated opportunities, particularly in non-high-tech industries. Finally, firms led by lobbyist CEOs exhibit lower future cost of goods sold, indicating improved operational efficiency, while they do not increase sales growth. Overall, the findings suggest that political capital substitutes for innovation in traditional industries but complements innovation and growth in technology-intensive sectors.

detail.abstract: Clustering-based statistical arbitrage makes two decisions, the clustering and the trading model, usually evaluated together. We separate them by trading 12 clusterizers and two controls, no clustering and a random partition, on 27 years of large US equities, under a fixed cross-sectional rule and a neural trading head. Clustering adds alpha and cuts book volatility by 28% to 42%, while the trading head adds primarily alpha. The clusterizers disagree on the groups yet trade closely correlated books; their Sharpe-ratio differences arise mainly through volatility. Most of the 12 clusterizers retain alpha that factors and per-stock peer regressions together cannot explain.

title: Market Dynamics and Policy Trade-offs in the Pharmaceutical Industry, in Nigeria

detail.title: Market Dynamics and Policy Trade-offs in the Pharmaceutical Industry, in Nigeria
detail.abstract: Nigeria's pharmaceutical sector is critical for health outcomes but faces severe constraints. Over 70% of medicines are imported, making the industry vulnerable to currency shocks. Recent exits of major firms like GSK, Unilever, which was attracbuted to riase in cost of production and naira volatility underscore these pressures. This study assesses how trade and investment policies affect sector performance, addressing challenges of import dependency and weak local capacity. We use annual data (2003-2023) on pharmaceutical output (profit before tax) and macro indicators (FDI inflows, monetary policy rate, exchange rate, labor force, health expenditure, tariffs). Econometric analyses include unit-root and cointegration tests, ordinary least squares regression, and an error-correction (ARDL) model to capture long-run relationships. We examine model diagnostics (VIF, autocorrelation) to ensure robustness. Exchange-rate volatility and trade barriers significantly hinder industry output. Regression results show that exchange rate depreciation has a strong negative effect on pharmaceutical profitability (p<0.01), and higher tariffs also suppress growth (p<0.05). In contrast, labor force growth is a powerful positive driver (p<0.001). Foreign direct investment (FDI) enters positively but is not statistically significant (p=0.18), suggesting structural or policy constraints on its efficacy. Health expenditure growth shows a small negative (marginal) impact, while higher interest rates unexpectedly correlate with better industry performance (p<0.05). The model explains a substantial share of output variance (adj. R² =0.57) and bounds testing confirms a long-run equilibrium among variables (F=12.37).

title: SDN-Enabled Dueling Deep Q-Network Mechanism for Energy-Efficient Task Offloading in Internet of Medical Things Applications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There was no conflict of interest in the study personal or financial.

The study did not used any published or secondary data. The study is an online Machine Learning study. A medical network environment was mathematically modelled for an AI agent to interact with; a discrete-events are generated
to mimic a medical setup and the model learns continuously from a stream of incoming live data, which are discarded after processing.

detail.abstract: The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) enables continuous, real-time monitoring of patient vital signs through wearable and bedside sensors, but the limited compute power and battery capacity of these devices make it challenging to process demanding diagnostic tasks locally. Offloading such tasks to remote cloud servers introduces network latency that can be clinically unacceptable, particularly for time-sensitive readings such as arrhythmia or hypoxic events. Existing offloading approaches either apply static, heuristic-based rules that cannot adapt to changing network conditions, or use deep reinforcement learning (DRL) that treats every task as equally important, with no regard to its clinical priority. This study addresses both limitations by proposing a Software-Defined Networking (SDN) enabled Dueling Deep Q-Network (Dueling DQN) framework for priority-aware task offloading in IoMT environments, in which the offloading agent is co-located with an SDN controller to exploit real-time, network-wide visibility, and physiological priority threshold classification is embedded directly into the state vector and reward function of a Markov Decision Process (MDP). The framework was evaluated through discrete-event simulation of a three-layer IoMT architecture, benchmarking against a Standard DQN baseline, Greedy and Round-Robin scheduling. Training and evaluation were repeated across 10 independent random seeds with variable network sizes to test average performance and robustness to network scale. The proposed Dueling DQN agent achieved up to a 95.5% reduction in average energy consumption per task relative to Greedy Scheduling, and recorded a 0.00% deadline violation rate for Tier-1 (most critical) tasks at every network size tested.

title: Reasoning More, Knowing No Better? Epistemic Calibration in Financial Reasoning Tasks
affiliations: , BlackRock, Inc, BlackRock, Inc, BlackRock, Inc, BlackRock, Inc, BlackRock, Inc, BlackRock, Inc, Independent and BlackRock, Inc

detail.title: Reasoning More, Knowing No Better? Epistemic Calibration in Financial Reasoning Tasks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The views expressed here are those of the authors alone and not of BlackRock, Inc.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reportedly 'reason' with increasing sophistication, but whether they 'know' when they are wrong remains poorly understood. We study epistemic calibration, the alignment between expressed confidence and empirical correctness, across approximately 30 contemporary models and configurable reasoning-effort budgets, using XFinBench (graduate-level financial reasoning) and SQuAD v2 (answerable and unanswerable questions). Reported confidence stays high relative to accuracy, with weak discrimination between correct and incorrect or unsupported answers. Miscalibration follows a Dunning-Kruger-like pattern: weaker models are often strongly overconfident, while frontier models are mildly underconfident. Reasoning effort significantly improves accuracy but has no detectable effect on the confidence-accuracy gap or ECE; stable between-model differences explain over 96% of calibration variance, versus a negligible effort effect. Calibration deteriorates most on scenario planning and numerical modeling. On SQuAD v2, models answer four in five unanswerable questions and remain near-maximally confident even when no answer is supported; higher reasoning effort yields no robust gain in calibration or abstention after multiplicity correction. We discuss implications for evaluation, deployment, and the design of calibration-aware, boundary-aware financial reasoning systems.

detail.abstract: Standard New Keynesian models treat aggregate total factor productivity as exogenous to monetary policy. This paper studies optimal monetary policy in the four-equation New Keynesian model of Baqaee, Farhi, and Sangani (2024), in which monetary expansions reallocate resources toward high-markup firms, reduce misallocation, and raise aggregate productivity. This endogenous productivity response flattens the Phillips curve and changes the optimal target criterion of a dual-mandate central bank. The resulting criterion is both forward- and backwardlooking. In my calibration, this criterion is closely approximated by a familiar New Keynesian target criterion adjusted only for the flatter Phillips curve. By contrast, applying a standard target criterion that ignores the effect of monetary policy on aggregate productivity leads the dual-mandate central bank to stabilize inflation too aggressively and generates excessive output fluctuations

detail.abstract: We decompose U.S. state labor-productivity growth over 1977-2024 into efficiency, technology, factor deepening, and a climate component, using a production-frontier decomposition disciplined by a panel-estimated temperature gradient. Against the cross country evidence, warming's incidence within the United States is flat: there is no cold dividend-colder years raise state output, a result that survives excluding utilities and heating-driven sectors-so the observed warming damaged every state (-0.2 to-0.8% of 44-year growth across weather-to-climate horizons), with no significant incidence gradient and no technology localization. The redistribution absent from output re-enters through capital: transmitting an engineering-estimated pavement damage function into climate-varying depreciation rates, we find 6-43% of the naive cross-state gradient in measured capital deepening is climate-δ mismeasurement-cold states' capital understated, warm states' overstated (correlation-0.94).

detail.abstract:
On March 18, 2025, the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors voted 7–2 to require a special exception before a data center could be built in the districts where the use had been permitted by right. That is close to consensus, it is the vote most accounts of the evening report, and it is narrower than it sounds.

The board adopted it over its own Planning Commission's recommendation of denial, forwarded 5–3–1 on December 12, 2024, carved out a grandfathered pipeline by a single vote, and left the standards it imposed modifiable through a lighter procedure opened two years earlier. It never reached the Route 28 corridor, where commercial and industrial zoning is frozen by state statute until 2037 and cannot be reduced by the board that adopted the reform, on a reading of the statute no court has construed and on which no Attorney General opinion was located on the search the volume's note 7 records. A point-geometry join this study cannot re-run puts 51 percent of Loudoun's built data center square footage inside that district, 43.16 percent of built and under-construction square footage, and 26.23 percent of what is under construction alone. The county publishes the constraint on its own website and names the governing Code subsection by letter; it went unmentioned across fourteen months of rewriting the ordinance, in the client alerts, the advocacy tracking and the fifteen transcripts examined here. It returned to contention in July and August 2026, and on September 1, 2026 the board sent the question to its lawyers.

The evening recorded nine dispositions. Two coalitions produced them: the members who opposed ending by-right development, and the members who supported ending it and thought the county had not gone far enough. The second group voted no on the grandfathering exemption and no again on the individual data center approval that followed. Those two minorities are nearly identical; only the ordinance minority stands apart from both.

Sixteen months later the new pathway had produced twenty-four legislative applications and exactly one public hearing. Fifteen of the twenty-four concern the delivery or generation of electricity, not the buildings that consume it. The grandfathered pipeline kept moving under a 1993 ordinance the county had spent two years replacing, and in February 2026 the Planning Commission processed a data center concept plan on which county staff stated on the record that data centers and substations were permitted without any special exception at all.

This case study documents what it costs to change the rules once the industry is load-bearing. Loudoun is the series' endgame case. Data center computer equipment revenue reached $879.1 million in the FY2027 adopted budget. No growth multiple is stated here, because the county did not break the figure out separately before tax year 2021 and the pre-2021 numbers in circulation measure a different population; the series starts at FY2022. In FY2027, the first year the county publishes both halves, data center personal and real property together account for roughly 40 percent of general fund revenue. The county's real property tax rate fell from $1.145 per $100 in tax year 2016 to $0.805 in 2025 and 2026. In 2016 Loudoun taxed residential property at a higher rate than Fairfax County did; by 2024 it taxed it twenty-six cents lower.

The volume is built from primary sources: fifteen locally transcribed public meetings, the county's own unauthenticated application database, nine annual comprehensive financial reports, adopted budgets, the commissioned transmission study, the appellate record, and the zoning ordinance text. Provisions that could not be retrieved are named, with what was attempted.

Three further findings run against the county's own account of itself. The board adopted a grandfathering standard without a stable count of what it was grandfathering: four staff-sourced counts, 36, then 50, then 21, then 31, moved across fifteen weeks with no bridge offered, and two were spoken under eight minutes apart in the same hearing from the same packet. No supervisor asked why the number had moved by half. Every count in the record is a floor, and county staff said so on the record: applications that do not name the use are not counted, and the county had by its own account once advised applicants not to name it. And the reform made the special exception mandatory without making the standards fixed: the county wrote explicit opt-out clauses into three other sections of its zoning ordinance, in two distinct formulations, and the data center standards carry neither, which leaves every applicable protection modifiable through the lighter pathway the 2023 rewrite had opened.

title: Value Contribution Measurement and the Reconstruction of Distributive Justice in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Theoretical Exploration Based on Public-Good Contribution

detail.title: Value Contribution Measurement and the Reconstruction of Distributive Justice in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Theoretical Exploration Based on Public-Good Contribution

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. No financial or personal relationships have influenced the work reported in this manuscript.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence and the platform economy are reshaping the relationship between labor, capital, and social value. Labor substitution, data monopoly, and wealth concentration have intensified the explanatory pressure on traditional distribution principles, while public-good contributions such as care work, education, and public health remain insufficiently recognized by market prices. Meanwhile, AI produces differential impacts across economies and labor groups, making international distributive inequality increasingly salient. To address this challenge, this article proposes public-good contribution as a supplementary reference dimension for distributive justice. Public-good contribution refers to the value created by actors through products, services, institutions, or actions that satisfy others' legitimate privategood needs and enhance social welfare. This concept is not limited to the narrow economic category of public goods (non-rivalrous, non-excludable goods); rather, it encompasses any activity that expands others' capabilities and social welfare, including private services with significant positive externalities. Drawing on the capability approach, public value theory, social impact assessment, and digital governance studies, this article constructs the Humanistic Value Model (HVM), which assesses public-good contribution through four dimensions: cognitive capacity, number of beneficiaries, duration of service, and depth of service. On this basis, the article designs a three-tier structure of distributive justice-dignity baseline, contribution incentives, and regulatory adjustment-ensuring basic dignity through baseline distribution, incentivizing genuine value creation through contribution-based distribution, and regulating monopoly, predatory, and speculative returns through constraint-based distribution. The article further proposes a negative externality regulation and public-good contribution compensation mechanism. This framework aims to provide a supplementary corrective lens for distributive justice in the age of AI, seeking a more reasonable institutional connection among technological progress, economic efficiency, and human dignity, while addressing AI-driven distributive inequality at both domestic and international levels.

detail.abstract:
On March 31, 2026, the Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed the judgment that had voided the Prince William Digital Gateway: three rezonings covering 1,760 acres of the county's Rural Crescent, approved by a lame-duck board at the end of a twenty-seven-hour hearing in December 2023, declared void ab initio because the county failed to follow its own public notice requirements. Two weeks later the Board of County Supervisors voted unanimously to stop defending the approvals it had once granted, after spending roughly $1.7 million in public money on the defense. Two weeks after that, Compass Datacenters walked away from the project. QTS, the remaining developer, filed a petition with the Supreme Court of Virginia three hours before the deadline, then withdrew it on July 2, 2026, announcing "a responsible wind-down." The largest data center proposal in American history is dead, and no court ever reached its merits.

This case study documents how the county got there, and why the route ran through a primary election, a general election, and three levels of the Virginia court system. Prince William is the case in this series where the governance itself was the failure point. A sitting supervisor signed a contract to sell his own land to one of the project's developers ten days before joining the application. The board chair held a disclosed position of $50,001 to $250,000 in the parent company of the other developer while the project moved through approval. The supervisor resigned under a conflict-of-interest ruling and was working for a data center lobbying firm within three months. The chair lost her primary to a political newcomer who ran against the project, then used the lame-duck period to push the rezonings through anyway. The voters corrected what the disclosure system could not. The courts then voided what the correction could not reach.

The study also documents what the correction did not end. After the new board was seated, a developer whose project a sitting supervisor had voted to approve made a $100,000 contribution to that supervisor's political action committee, described by the Prince William Times as likely the largest from an individual donor to any supervisor in county history, followed by a second $100,000 from another data center landowner. The lobbying firm that hired the resigned supervisor filed a comprehensive plan amendment for a 1,940-acre assemblage that would rival the Digital Gateway, and now employs a sitting School Board member. The county that voided the flagship project collected $293.7 million in data center tax revenue in 2024, raised its equipment rate to $4.50 per $100 in April 2026, the highest in Northern Virginia, and adopted a budget that projects roughly $550 million in data center revenue, paying for a residential tax cut. Whether democratic correction is durable or merely cyclical is the sharpest question the institutional behavior framework confronts anywhere in this series. Prince William supplies evidence on both sides, and this study does not resolve what the record leaves unresolved.

detail.abstract: Objectives: Roadside intersection safety systems generate heterogeneous sensor streams that are difficult to synchronize, validate, interpret, and translate into actionable safety information. This study develops a reproducible framework that transforms multisensor roadside recordings into synchronized, replayable representations, traceable safety-event products, fleet-level reports, and grounded operator advisories. Methods: The framework was evaluated using 41 validation runs from the United States Department of Transportation Intersection Safety Challenge Stage 1B dataset. Ground-truth trajectories, two LiDAR streams, four radar streams when available, camera timing, and signal data were aligned within a common spatial and temporal reference. The synchronized representation supported event extraction, fleet-level analysis, and operator advisories generated by a fine-tuned language model. Findings: The framework successfully processed all validation runs, including those with missing sensor modalities, at approximately 20 runs per hour. It identified a fleet-wide radar elevation misalignment, concentrated predicted conflicts within a small subset of runs, and resolved the dataset's ground-truth coordinate-frame interpretation, reducing the LiDARto-ground-truth residual from 8.32 m to 0.89 m. The advisory model achieved an nDCG@5 of 0.74, Kendall's T of 0.83, and a grounding rate of 0.81, although operator oversight remains necessary because of a 0.24 hallucination rate. Novelty: The study contributes a reproducible multisensor framework that integrates synchronization, visualization, traceable event abstraction, fleet-level reporting, validated coordinate-frame interpretation, and grounded language-model advisories within a single workflow for roadside intersection data. Practical Applications: The framework provides transportation agencies with a repeatable workflow for reviewing recorded multisensor data, identifying sensor-health issues, screening data quality, prioritizing safety-critical scenarios for human review, and supporting digital-twin data validation before downstream operational analyses.

detail.abstract:
Data centers in the United States often buy treated water from a public utility rather
than pumping their own. Virginia and Tennessee treat such a facility, by express
rule, as a customer rather than a withdrawer of water, and Georgia’s surface water
statute does the same, its groundwater clause being left open here, so the only report
of its consumption that reaches the state is the utility’s own. This article reads the
reporting forms the three states prescribe, field by field, and shows that none of the
four recurring forms, in the revisions read, provides a field built for a customer of
this kind. Virginia’s form records a sale of water between two waterworks and has
no field for the other party. Tennessee’s asks a buyer to name its source and asks a
seller nothing about its buyers. Georgia’s alone ask a seller to identify its buyer, and
the field is built for another water system. The reading is of the published paper forms;
the three states’ electronic filing systems were not accessed. The finding is placed in
the literature on how water use comes to be measured, or not, and on the legibility of
water consumers to the state: the three states invert the western pattern Kroepsch
describes, since the volume is measured and it is the recipient the record cannot see.
The article closes with the 2026 record, in which Virginia’s General Assembly added
a field to the utility’s report and left the definition of a withdrawer where it stood.

title: Beyond the Scorecard: A Framework for Detecting False-positive Product-market Fit in Pre-seed and Seed-stage Ventures

detail.abstract:
Pre-seed and seed-stage capital allocation still relies on tools built for a pre-AI, single-
region market. The Scorecard Method (Payne, 2001; revised 2019) and the TABS Score
(2019) remain the most cited named frameworks in angel and early-stage due
diligence, and neither was designed to separate self-reported founder enthusiasm
from evidenced traction, nor to operate across the deal-structure differences that now
separate North American SAFE-dominated pre-seed rounds from the Convertible
Loan Agreements and Advance Subscription Agreements common in Europe, and the
free-zone equity structures of the GCC. This gap has become material: seed-to-
Series-A conversion for the 2022–2023 cohort fell to roughly 15%, down from over 30%
for 2018–2020 cohorts, median time between seed and Series A has stretched toward
616 days, and 2026 investors are increasingly explicit about rejecting what they
describe as “false positives” of product-market fit — traction signals that read as
validation but do not survive institutional scrutiny. This paper introduces KVEX 10.1, an
AI-orchestrated investability diagnostic that extends the KVEX v10.0 framework (Khan,
2026) with an explicit false-positive PMF detection layer, evidence-graded scoring,
and a native regional adaptation model spanning North America, the GCC, and
Europe. The framework is illustrated through three anonymized regional case
applications — North America, GCC, and Europe — governed by NDA confidentiality
protocol, in which a high-presentation traction claim (average self-reported
presentation score of approximately 9.2/10 across the three cases) was in every case
capped by a materially weaker evidence grade once verified, ranging from partial
structural blockers to unverified self-reported pipeline. For founders, angels, and early-
stage funds operating in a 2026 market the venture industry itself is calling a
correction year after two years of hype-funded deals, this has direct implications for
how investability should be assessed before capital changes hands. Version note:
KVEX 10.1 (2026) extends v10.0 (Khan, 2026) by removing Modes 5 (PARTNERS) and 7 (VC
FINDER), renumbering the remaining six modes, retaining the 12-factor investability
diagnostic under the name Idea Validation Report, and confirming the regional
adaptation layer for North America, GCC, and Europe.

title: Learning Passibility: Causal World Models for Hidden Paths, False Paths, and Transformative Actions

detail.title: Learning Passibility: Causal World Models for Hidden Paths, False Paths, and Transformative Actions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interests
declarations.funderStatement: no funding

detail.abstract: A world model answers one question: given this action, what happens next? We ask a second one: given what the agent knows and can do, which actions are really possible, which only look possible, which are possible and unseen, and which become possible after an enabling step. We call this structure passibility and we test, with matched experiments, whether learning it explicitly adds anything to a conventional world model. Five findings. (1) The passibility of the specific action about to be taken is the most informative signal about whether that action will be wasted: adding it to the conventional signals raises auc from 0.878 to 0.989 in distribution and from 0.822 to 0.899 under structural shift. (2) Every scalar summary of that structure-an availability count, the programme's Perception and Freedom scalars, a value estimate-loses 0.07 to 0.13 auc: the information lives in which action is open, hidden or false, and vanishes when counted. (3) A conventional world model already holds this structure in its posterior state: a small nonlinear probe reads it out at least as well as an explicit head, so the head is a readout rather than a new representation. (4) In an environment where a wrong step costs one move, a planner that tries and replans beats a planner that predicts and vetoes: the learned veto removes a third to a half of wasted actions and lowers success by 6 to 17 points, because a wrong veto loses a route while a false path loses a step; the cost asymmetry, not the accuracy, decides. (5) The causal reading of the guard-gated field-do(door := open) propagating to every guarded action-is unidentified in this version, because the world term absorbs the guard state from the observation; the fix is named. The paper closes with a recipe for using passibility in language-model agents and robots-as a calibrated readout for ranking, asking and probing, and as an evaluation metric where false-path rate is action hallucination and hidden-path recall is blindness-and with four pre-committed tests that can fail. Everything here stands independently of the Architecture of Freedom Intelligence programme that motivated it.

detail.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves language-model usefulness by supplying external evidence, but it also creates a governance problem that ordinary access-control metadata does not fully solve. A system may authenticate a principal correctly and still retrieve evidence that is stale, outside the permitted scope, subject to retention or legal-hold constraints, or inconsistent with the authority state at request time. TenantSage is proposed as a governance-execution architecture in which authority and policy constrain the admissible evidence universe before semantic retrieval is permitted. The architecture separates the hard customer boundary from an internal AuthorityScope hierarchy, requires an explicit active scope, constructs and seals an Eligible Evidence Boundary (EEB), and allows relevance mechanisms to rank or reduce that boundary but not enlarge it. It further separates durable retrieval admission, governed context, pre-generation ledger commitment, model generation, response validation, and externally consequential execution. The manuscript defines the S0-S8 pipeline, typed DENY and FAILED outcomes, temporal and freshness invariants, source-tochunk governance inheritance, database-enforcement expectations, AI visibility boundaries, and a conformance-evidence model. TenantSage is presented as a falsifiable architecture and verification programme, not as proof of deployed security, formal correctness, regulatory certification, independent assurance, or measured performance.

title: Quantile Meets Mean: Robust Pricing under Bounded Residual Surplus
affiliations: Georgia  Institute  of  Technology, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics and Georgia  Institute  of  Technology

detail.title: Quantile Meets Mean: Robust Pricing under Bounded Residual Surplus

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Sellers often price with only coarse demand information, such as average willingness to pay and the conversion rate at one tested price. These statistics capture complementary aspects of demand: the mean measures aggregate market value, whereas the quantile anchors demand at a specific price. Yet in robust pricing this complementarity is illusory: without additional structure on the valuation distribution, an adversary can match both statistics while hiding any additional mean in an equal-revenue tail, so the mean cannot improve the worst-case guarantee beyond the observed quantile. This phenomenon reflects a broader challenge in statistics-based robust optimization, in which worst-case guarantees can be driven by extremal distributions-such as two-or few-point laws or arbitrarily long equal-revenue tails-that match the known statistics but allocate value in economically extreme ways. It motivates a more structured ambiguity set that preserves the usability of coarse statistics while ruling out implausible tail behavior. We introduce bounded residual surplus (BRS), a distributional condition for robust pricing: conditional on accepting any price, a buyer's expected residual willingness to pay is at most the ex ante mean. This condition links residualtail behavior to the mean without relying on local hazard-rate assumptions. The BRS class contains all monotone-hazard-rate distributions, admits atoms and discrete distributions, and, once the mean is fixed, induces a convex ambiguity set. For BRS distributions, we solve the robust randomized pricing problem under mean information, quantile information, and their combination. The solution shows precisely when the mean is valuable, how it reshapes the optimal randomized pricing rule, and when the two constraints jointly yield a new deterministic robust price. The analysis identifies how a global measure of market value and local demand observations are linked through residual-tail geometry.

title: DAOs as Holacracies? Comparing Decentralized Governance Structures Through an Organizational Theory Lens
affiliations: ClimateActionX

detail.title: DAOs as Holacracies? Comparing Decentralized Governance Structures Through an Organizational Theory Lens

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship and/or publication of this article.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Holacracy and Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) are both advanced as alternatives to managerial hierarchy, yet organizational theory has rarely placed them in direct dialogue: Holacracy has developed within management and organizational behavior scholarship, DAOs within blockchain, computer science and political economy research. This paper closes that gap by comparing the two governance forms across six theoretically grounded dimensions—authority distribution, decision mechanism, membership and inclusion, accountability, transparency and adaptability—drawing on self-managing organizations theory, open strategy scholarship and blockchain governance research. The analysis shows that although both structures pursue decentralized authority, they instantiate it through opposing logics: Holacracy through socially mediated, constitutional consent processes, and DAOs through algorithmically enforced, token-weighted voting. These divergent logics generate distinct pathologies—role ambiguity and captured consent in Holacracy; token concentration and participatory apathy in DAOs—that this paper interprets as structurally analogous manifestations of the transparency–inclusion tension identified in open strategy research. Building on this comparison, three theoretical propositions are advanced concerning governance convergence, the distinct bases of procedural versus outcome-based legitimacy, and the contextual conditions under which each model is likely to be effective. A resulting governance typology situates Holacracy and DAOs among hierarchical, sociocratic and wirearchic forms. The paper contributes to organizational theory by identifying socially-embedded and algorithmically-embedded decentralization as a previously undertheorized distinction, and by offering blockchain governance scholars organizational-theoretic tools—including Ostrom's institutional design principles—for interpreting DAO governance failures.

detail.abstract: AI agents can already discover services. What they cannot obtain is a record of how a service behaved that the service did not author. Scores and rankings fill that gap today, and scores are gameable by construction. NENRIN is a public, Bitcoin-anchored record of conduct for agent-facing services (Model Context Protocol servers and similar endpoints) built on counts rather than scores. Its third layer, the ring, bundles one calendar month of measured history for one endpoint into one file: how many times it was sampled, how many times it answered, how many distinct tool surfaces were observed, how many independent witnesses measured it, and what the record cannot say. The specification claims that anyone holding the same history can rebuild the ring byte for byte. This paper tests that claim the hard way. A second implementer, who had executed the reference builder as a black box but had not read its body, wrote a builder in a different language (Node.js) from the anchored specification and the published ring files, and ran it against the eight published August 2026 rings. All eight reproduced byte for byte, and both results were anchored (JIDEC entries 32 and 34). The exercise surfaced one seam that a naive port would have crossed without noticing: the specification does not state the canonical form at all, so nested key ordering was inherited from a language runtime and reached the second implementer through the published artifacts rather than through the specification. We report the protocol, the eight matches, the seam and its class, and the limits: byte reproducibility proves that the ring layer is deterministic, not that the measurements inside it are true; two implementations are not a community; the August rings carry a single witness. A blind rerun against the September rings, which will be the first to include a second witness, is pre-registered here.

title: Optimal Control of Matching Queues
affiliations: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Columbia University and Hong Kong Polytechnic University

detail.title: Optimal Control of Matching Queues

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This work was supported by general research grants. The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: NSFC and HK/RGC

detail.abstract: Multiple classes of jobs arrive at a matching system following renewal processes. Each class has its own matching scheme-what jobs from other classes are needed to form a match. The decision is whether to match the jobs that are currently in their buffers and hence remove them from the queues (instantaneously), or to wait for further arrivals with the hope to form better matches later. The objective is to minimize a long-run average holding cost of jobs waiting in their buffers. We first identify a critically-loaded condition, under which our matching queue system converges (weakly) to a diffusion limit that can be expressed as a dynamic linearcomplementarity problem, also known as the Skorohod Problem (SP). The SP connects to a reflected Brownian motion (RBM) control problem that can be explicitly solved. The optimal reflection control is then methodically translated into a cyclic review-matching policy, with the review-cycle length depending on the variability of the interarrival times, and the optimal number of matches per cycle solved from a constrained convex optimization problem. Finally, we show this cyclic matching policy to be optimal for the original system under the critically-loaded condition.

title: Black Belt Banking: Emancipation and the Geography of Southern Credit

detail.abstract: Antebellum Southern credit relied on enslaved people as collateral, an arrangement emancipation ended in 1865. We show that emancipation reversed financial development for a century and a half. In a county panel of Confederate states from 1820 to 2024, a one-standard-deviation higher 1860 slave share predicts 64 percent more banks before emancipation but 51 percent fewer afterward, and 31 percent fewer still today. Regulations lowering bank capital requirements increased bank entry, but branching deregulation did not eliminate the gap. A modern-day movers design shows that living in these counties changes credit access, but not credit risk.

title: The Derived Demand for Sawtimber as a Nonallocable Factor of Stochastic Production
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Derived Demand for Sawtimber as a Nonallocable Factor of Stochastic Production

declarations.declarationOfInterest: David Rossi provides market research and consulting services for the forest products sector.

detail.abstract: Sawtimber represents a critical feedstock to both the lumber manufacturing sector and the pulp, paper, and bioenergy sectors since the byproducts from lumber production are typically sold as a substitute for pulpwood feedstocks when not re-utilized by sawmills for energy production. To explore a sawmill's sensitivities to changing prices, the demand function for sawtimber is derived as a nonallocable factor using a stylized model of lumber production under risk. A numerical simulation model is developed to approximate the expected percentage change in annual sawtimber demanded given percentage changes in residue prices for a southern pine lumber mill operating in North Carolina. This is found to be an inelastic response: a one percent increase in residue prices is expected to raise sawtimber demand by less than one percent. In contrast, sawtimber demand is elastic with respect to lumber prices: a one percent increase in the lumber price raises sawtimber demand by more than one percent. The model also enables an examination of the net effects from simultaneous changes in lumber prices, residue prices, and wage rates. These cross-price elasticities show the potential for inverse price changes across lumber and wood residue markets to offset each other and stabilize the sawmill's annual demand for timber. This potential is found to be limited under current prices.

detail.abstract: We study the execution of externally supplied replenishment policies in a dual-sourcing inventory system with deterministic lead times, backlogging, nonnegative orders and irrevocable pipelines. Switching back to an incumbent policy does not restore its inventory state, so fixed deviation constraints can become infeasible. We construct a bounded-deviation execution rule that relaxes inventory-position upper bounds sequentially while preserving lower bounds and order feasibility. A pipeline invariant yields a finite-horizon excess-cost guarantee on every nonnegative demand path, without assumptions on advice quality. The same state bounds support reusable certificates for finite menus of executed actions on a fixed lattice. These certificates cover arbitrary history-dependent mode selection without enumerating private controller memory. On the certified physical-state graph, nominal verification inequalities bound the improvement available from further controller design, and a regime-change bound separates inference losses from inventory transients. Exact arithmetic and independent simulation comparisons show that a larger admissible action set need not provide economically useful flexibility; useful updates require modes suited to different demand conditions. Jointly optimized direct controllers remain competitive and often cheaper in the evaluated finite searches. The contribution is a recursively feasible inventory execution method and a framework for distinguishing feasible action freedom, risk evidence and conditional performance improvements. Exact absolute risk statements remain conditional on the specified demand domain; the pathwise relative guarantee does not require that restriction.

detail.abstract: National innovation-system (NIS) research offers structural, functional, and transformational diagnoses, yet policy design still requires deeper specification of why observed dysfunctions persist. This article develops an institution-focused diagnostic architecture that connects established innovation system problem analysis with the Viable System Model (VSM). Rather than mapping failure categories one-to-one onto VSM systems, the framework treats observed dysfunctions as entry points for testing alternative explanations involving identity, operational autonomy, coordination, cohesion, monitoring, intelligence, policy, recursion, and requisite variety. A four-layer architecture links manifestations, established NIS diagnoses, VSM inquiry, and hypothesized viability mechanisms before moving to policy or institutional redesign. A bounded documentary illustration using Iran's science, technology and innovation governance shows how similar manifestations can imply different regulatory causes and therefore different intervention logics. The article contributes a mechanism-oriented diagnostic bridge intended to improve causal specification prior to instrument choice and policy-mix design.

detail.abstract: This article develops a mid-range theoretical framework explaining how localized instability in Eurasian peripheries generates asymmetric systemic effects in the emerging multipolar international order. Three analytically distinct constructs are introduced. Ordered Disorder (OD) denotes a structurally persistent condition in which peripheral instability is continuously reproduced without converging toward full resolution or systemic collapsean emergent property of complex systemic interaction rather than of centralized strategic design. Peripheral Pressure Transfer (PPT) specifies the causal mechanism through which peripheral disruptions propagate toward strategic cores via five coupled transmission channels: energy markets, maritime chokepoints, trade corridors, financial systems, and alliance realignments. Strategic Agency Modulation (SAM) reconceptualizes buffer states as adaptive actors whose counter-containment strategies transform the PPT architecture from a linear transmission model into a recursive adaptive network, introducing genuine blowback dynamics.

title: Porter's Five Forces in the Age of Generative and Agentic AI: A Structural Reassessment of Competitive Strategy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not Applicable.

detail.abstract: Michael Porter's Five Forces framework (Porter, 1979) has anchored competitive strategy analysis for over four decades, providing a structural account of how the threat of new entrants, supplier power, buyer power, substitution risk, and competitive rivalry jointly determine industry profitability. The recent, rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and autonomous, toolusing agentic AI systems constitutes a structural shock to each of these five forces simultaneously. This paper offers a systematic, force-by-force reassessment of Porter's model in light of GenAI and Agentic AI, arguing that while the analytical structure of the framework remains valid, the empirical weight and directionality of several forces have shifted materially since 2023. We synthesize observed enterprise adoption patterns into a qualitative disruption-intensity comparison across the five forces, distinguishing the effects of content-generating (GenAI) versus autonomous, executioncapable (Agentic AI) systems. We find that Agentic AI exerts a systematically larger structural effect than GenAI alone on every force, most acutely on buyer bargaining power and competitive rivalry, because it automates execution rather than merely content production. We conclude with strategic implications for practitioners and researchers, and note the limitations of a qualitative, practitionerinformed synthesis of this kind.

title: Bayesian Learning of Demand and Stockout-Based Substitution for Risk-Aware Inventory Optimization
affiliations: , HEC Montréal and HEC Montreal

detail.title: Bayesian Learning of Demand and Stockout-Based Substitution for Risk-Aware Inventory Optimization

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported in part by funding from IVADO (Institute for Data Valorization).

keywords: risk-aware inventory optimization Bayesian Learning for Risk-Aware Inventory Optimization

detail.abstract:
Problem definition: Risk-aware inventory management for substitutable products is highly challenging as stockouts and substitutions couple inventory risk across products. In practice, however, retailers observe only transaction and inventory records, while customer arrivals, first-choice preferences, substitution decisions, and lost sales remain unobserved. We study how to learn a probabilistic generative model of latent demand and stockout-based substitution from censored transaction data and incorporate the resulting uncertainty into risk-aware replenishment decisions.

Methodology/results: We develop a Bayesian model in which completed purchases form a state-dependent marked point process whose mark-specific intensities depend on the inventory availability path reconstructed from transactions. A nonhomogeneous Poisson arrival process, with a covariate-driven period-level intensity and a within-period arrival profile, is combined with a sequential first-choice and substitution process. We propose a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling method to derive the posterior distributions of model parameters. We then simulate the profit distribution under a periodic-review replenishment system and search for order-up-to policies under a mean conditional value at risk (mean-CVaR) objective. On simulated data and two real datasets, the model improves predictive accuracy over benchmarks in the literature, and the risk-aware policy improves lower-tail profit relative to risk-neutral, no-substitution, and plug-in benchmarks.

Managerial implications: Transaction timing records contain valuable information that aggregate sales do not capture. Our experiments show that this information improves demand prediction and that accounting for substitution and estimation uncertainty improves lower-tail profit relative to policies that overlook substitution, rely on point estimates, or optimize expected profit alone. The results highlight the value of integrating demand and substitution learning, uncertainty quantification, and risk-aware inventory optimization.

title: Organizational Representation and Operational Reality in Planned Enterprise Transformation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: Planned enterprise transformation requires consequential decisions while operational conditions, information flows, systems, roles, and measures may themselves be changing. This study examines the relationship between decision-relevant operational conditions and the organizational representations available to decision-makers during transformation. The primary research question asks under what conditions the organizational representation of planned enterprise transformation available to decision-makers aligns with or diverges from the decisionrelevant operational conditions of the transformation. Using a qualitative longitudinal multiplecase design, the study reconstructs consequential transformation decision episodes across four historical enterprise transformation cases. For each episode, the decision-relevant operational condition (O_t) and the decision-level organizational representation (R_t) are reconstructed independently and bounded to the pre-decision evidentiary window before correspondence is assessed. Managerial interpretation, consequential decision, subsequent operational condition, and changes in organizational observability are analyzed separately. The method preserves contradictory evidence, rival explanations, ambiguity, and indeterminacy and prohibits later outcomes from being projected backward into earlier decision states. Across the four qualifying cases, the correspondence determinations showed substantial alignment at the bounded decision points, including corrective movement after operational evidence entered the decision process and progressive construction of representation through investigation, elicitation, verification, reconciliation, and review. No defensible material-divergence case was identified, and earlier states lacking sufficient evidence remained unclassified rather than being retrospectively converted into divergence. The cross-case analysis indicates that correspondence is temporally dynamic and that representations are constructed rather than merely transmitted. Transformation activity can also alter organizational observability, most clearly where new investigation, integration, verification, or structured representation makes previously dispersed or uncertain conditions more visible to decision-making. The dissertation contributes to a decision-bounded relational and methodological configuration for studying correspondence between operational conditions and decision-level organizational representations. It further develops representational corrective capacity as a candidate construct describing the organizational capacity for new, contradictory, refined, or previously unrepresented operational evidence to enter a consequential decision process and modify the representation available to decision-makers. The findings do not establish that alignment causes transformation success and do not generalize material divergence beyond the evidence observed. Instead, they provide a controlled framework for investigating how operational reality becomes represented, revised, and acted upon during enterprise transformation.

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is transforming how organizations manage knowledge, but its implications for knowledge integration have yet to be fully understood. This study examines how generative AI enables organizations to integrate tacit knowledge at scale and identifies the conditions under which these approaches work well. We conducted a grounded theory study with 66 semi-structured interviews across 52 organizations implementing generative AI in knowledgeintensive work. Our analysis reveals a three-stage process: organizational preparation, AI-enabled integration, and capability emergence. We find that pattern-based mediation serves as a key mechanism in the integration stage-AI learns context-action patterns from observing how experts work and then applies this knowledge throughout the organization. This differs from traditional approaches that require experts to explicitly document their knowledge or spend extensive time coordinating with others. Our findings suggest this mechanism offers organizations new ways to leverage deep expertise more broadly while maintaining its strategic value. However, success depends on specific boundary conditions. Our study contributes to understanding how generative AI reshapes organizational knowledge integration possibilities while specifying where these mechanisms work effectively and where they face constraints.

detail.abstract: Founder-led organizations often scale faster than their decision systems. Early in a venture, concentrated judgment can be an advantage because the founder carries context, accepts ambiguity, and can resolve tradeoffs without extensive coordination. As the organization grows, however, the same concentration can produce decision latency, repeated escalation, inconsistent delegation, and a widening gap between formal roles and real authority. This conceptual paper develops a decision-architecture framework for moving critical decisions beyond continuous founder involvement without treating decentralization as an end in itself. Decision architecture is defined here as the designed arrangement through which an organization classifies decisions, allocates decision rights, routes information, sets thresholds and guardrails, specifies escalation paths, assigns accountability, captures feedback, and converts repeated judgment into institutional learning. Drawing on research on bounded rationality, authority, information processing, organizational learning, resource allocation, and founder transition, the paper proposes an eight-element Decision Architecture Chain and a five-stage maturity model ranging from founder omnipresence to adaptive institutional decision systems. Six propositions specify how alignment among information locality, decision rights, escalation, accountability, and learning should affect decision speed, control, and organizational adaptability. The core argument is that scalable decision making is not achieved by removing the founder from decisions indiscriminately. It is achieved by redesigning the system so that routine judgment becomes repeatable, exceptional judgment becomes visible, and genuinely strategic judgment remains concentrated where its value is highest. The framework offers a research agenda and a practical diagnostic for founders, executives, boards, and investors seeking to build organizations that can act coherently without requiring constant founder intervention.

title: A First-Order Learning Algorithm for Online Resource Allocation with Constant Regret

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: We study a finite-horizon online resource allocation problem with initial resource capacities proportional to the horizon. In each period, a request type is observed and one action is chosen from a finite menu. Each action earns a reward and consumes a vector of resources. The arrival types are independent and identically distributed, but their probabilities are unknown. We present a primal first-order learning policy that, in each period, performs one gradient ascent update of the action coordinates associated with the current request type. The policy achieves O(1) expected additive regret relative to the hindsight optimum, with a bound independent of the horizon T. It does not solve any linear program, and the regret bound does not require a nondegeneracy assumption on the fluid linear program.

detail.abstract: Contemporary cyber-physical systems—spanning from sub-millisecond kinetic Edge AI to decadal scientific R&D (AI4S)—are trapped in a verification paradox: novel discoveries require low-cost verification to incubate, but establishing the initial physical anchor demands massive capital. This concluding paper of the Governance Operating System (GOS) tetralogy resolves this bottleneck by operationalizing the framework as a dynamic Configuration Management (CM) baseline. Utilizing an 8-Dimensional Deployment Matrix, we map the hardware and governance boundaries required across diverse physical domains. We introduce the Verification Ratchet: by decomposing high-entropy cloud proposals and verifying them locally against deterministic physical anchors, every result—including intercepted failures—is minted into an immutable WORM Ledger. This transforms research into compounding sovereign assets, structurally driving the marginal cost of subsequent explorations down toward a thermodynamic floor. Finally, we introduce the "Third Route" to intellectual property—verifiable provenance without content disclosure—bypassing Arrow’s Information Paradox and enabling cross-sovereign knowledge integration.

detail.abstract: Prior research has examined audit firms' expansion into new assurance areas but offers limited insight into the process by which they prepare for, and decide on, market entry. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities framework and evidence from interviews, firm disclosures, and job postings in the technologically complex and high-risk setting of blockchain audits, we develop a three-phase process model-experimenting, preparing, and applying-of how audit firms build the capabilities needed to decide whether to enter a new audit space. The process is recursive: path dependencies and frictions rooted in risk aversion and the profession's regulated character slow, and can reverse, progress. Beyond theorizing capability building prior to the entry decision, we show that the dynamic capabilities framework requires modification for knowledge-based professional service firms, whose expansion is governed by reputation and professional jurisdiction rather than by the physical assets of the settings in which the framework was built.
